104279.q: What is yellow bone marrow also called?
104279.e: Because it contains so much fat, it is also called fatty marrow. The spinal cord, by contrast, is part of the nervous system.
104279.m: Yellow bone marrow is also called fatty marrow.

104280.q: In adults, where is yellow bone marrow mainly found?
a: In the marrow cavity of the long bones
104280.e: In adults, the marrow in the shaft of the thighbone, humerus and other long bones is mostly yellow.
104280.m: In adults, the shafts of long bones are filled with fatty marrow.

104281.q: How does bone marrow change over a lifetime?
a: Red marrow gradually turns into yellow marrow
Yellow marrow gradually turns into red marrow
104281.e: With age, the blood-forming marrow in many bones is gradually replaced by fatty marrow. This change already begins in childhood.
104281.m: With age, red marrow turns into yellow marrow.

104282.q: What can yellow bone marrow do after a large loss of blood?
a: It can turn back into blood-forming marrow
104282.e: If the body urgently needs many new blood cells, fatty marrow can turn back into red, blood-forming marrow.
104282.m: Yellow marrow is a reserve for making blood.

104283.q: What is one job of the fat in yellow bone marrow?
a: It serves as an energy store
104283.e: The fat in bone marrow is one of the body’s energy reserves. Newer research shows that it also releases messenger substances.

104284.q: Which dish made from veal shank has a slice of bone with marrow in the middle?
104284.e: Ossobuco means “bone with a hole” in Italian. The hole is the marrow cavity, filled with soft fatty marrow.
104284.m: In ossobuco you can see the marrow cavity of a long bone.

104285.q: In adults, roughly what share of the bone marrow is yellow marrow?
104285.e: In adults, red and yellow marrow are present in roughly equal amounts. In old age the yellow share increases further.
104285.m: In adults, about half of the bone marrow is fatty marrow.

a: On the outside of the bone
104286.e: The periosteum covers the bone on the outside like a thin sleeve. Only the joint surfaces are free of it.
104286.m: The periosteum wraps the bone on the outside.

104287.q: Why does a knock on the edge of the shin hurt so much?
a: The periosteum is full of nerves
The bone itself is very soft
The skin is especially thick there
104287.e: At the edge of the shin, the periosteum lies almost directly under the skin. It contains a great many pain fibres.
104287.m: The periosteum is very sensitive to pain.

104288.q: What does the periosteum contain to supply the bone?
104288.e: Blood vessels run from the periosteum into the bone. They bring oxygen and nutrients.
104288.m: The bone is supplied with blood through the periosteum.

104289.q: Which kind of bone growth is the periosteum important for?
104289.e: The inner layer of the periosteum contains bone-forming cells. They add new bone tissue on the outside, so the bone gets thicker.
104289.m: The periosteum makes bone grow thicker.

104290.q: What is the periosteum made of?
104290.e: The periosteum is a tough skin of connective tissue. It is firmly anchored in the bone with fine fibres.
104290.m: The periosteum is made of tough connective tissue.

104291.q: Where is a bone not covered by periosteum?
a: On the shaft of the bone
On the edge of the shin
On the top of the skull
104291.e: The joint surfaces are covered with smooth cartilage. There is no periosteum there.
104291.m: Joint surfaces have cartilage instead of periosteum.

104292.q: Which complaint often affects runners’ shins?
104292.e: With overuse, the periosteum on the shin can become inflamed. Pain along the inner edge is typical.
104292.m: Too much running training can irritate the periosteum on the shin.

104293.q: What role does the periosteum play when a bone breaks?
a: Its cells help make new bone
104293.e: After a fracture, the bone-forming cells of the periosteum become active and help to bridge the break.

104294.q: What tissue is the growth plate made of?
104294.e: The growth plate is a disc of cartilage. Its cartilage cells multiply and are turned into bone on the shaft side.
104294.m: The growth plate is a disc of cartilage.

104295.q: What are growth plates responsible for?
104295.e: At the growth plates, the long bones of children and teenagers get longer.
104295.m: Bones grow in length at the growth plates.

104296.q: How can you recognise the growth plates on a child’s X-ray?
a: As a narrow gap near the end of the bone
As a bright spot in the middle of the shaft
As a dark ring around the joint
104296.e: Growth plates are made of cartilage. That is why on an X-ray they appear as a narrow gap near the end of the bone.
104296.m: On an X-ray, growth plates appear as a narrow gap.

104297.q: Where is the growth plate of a long bone?
a: Between the end of the bone and the shaft
In the middle of the shaft
104297.e: It lies near both ends of a long bone, between the joint end and the shaft.
104297.m: The growth plates are near the ends of the bone.

104298.q: How can a doctor estimate how much more a child will grow?
a: With an X-ray of the hand
104298.e: An X-ray of the hand shows how far the growth plates have already closed. From this the bone age is worked out.
104298.m: Bone age is read from an X-ray of the hand.

104299.q: At what age do most growth plates close?
a: Towards the end of the teenage years
104299.e: At the end of growth, the cartilage discs turn completely into bone, usually between about 15 and 20. After that, bones no longer grow in length.
104299.m: Once the growth plates have closed, you don’t get any taller.

104300.q: Why must an injury to a growth plate in children be treated especially carefully?
104300.e: If the growth plate is damaged, the bone can grow too short or crooked. That is why such fractures are checked carefully.
104300.m: Growth plate injuries can change growth.

104301.q: Which hormone especially stimulates growth at the growth plates?
104301.e: Growth hormone is made in the pituitary gland. It helps the cartilage cells in the growth plates multiply.
104301.m: Growth hormone drives growth in length.

104302.q: Why does cartilage damage heal only very slowly?
104302.e: Cartilage has no direct blood supply but is nourished through fluid. That is why there are not enough cells and nutrients for quick healing.
104302.m: Without blood vessels, cartilage heals poorly.

104303.q: How does cartilage feel compared with bone?
104303.e: Cartilage is firm but elastic. You can feel it in your outer ear or the tip of your nose.
104303.m: Cartilage is softer and more bendy than bone.

104304.q: Which type of cartilage gives the outer ear its shape?
104304.e: Elastic cartilage can bend and spring back into shape. That is why you can fold your ear over without it breaking.
104304.m: The outer ear is made of elastic cartilage.

a: In the tip of the nose
104305.e: The discs lie between the vertebral bodies of the spine. Their tough ring of cartilage cushions shocks.

104306.q: What does the smooth cartilage on joint surfaces do?
a: It reduces friction in the joint
104306.e: Joint cartilage is smooth and slightly springy. Together with the joint fluid, it lets the bones glide almost without friction.
104306.m: Joint cartilage lets the bones glide easily.

104307.q: Which part of the face is mainly supported by cartilage?
104307.e: The upper part of the nose is bone, but the tip and the sides of the nostrils are cartilage. That is why the tip of your nose can move.
104307.m: The movable tip of the nose is made of cartilage.

104308.q: Which animals have a skeleton made almost entirely of cartilage?
104308.e: Sharks and rays are cartilaginous fish. Their skeleton doesn’t turn into bone but is still stable.

104309.q: What is much of an unborn child’s skeleton made of at first?
104309.e: Many bones are first laid down as a cartilage model. This is gradually replaced by bone, which is called ossification.
104309.m: Many bones develop from a cartilage model.

104310.q: Which group of substances does collagen belong to?
104310.e: Collagen is a fibrous protein. It forms long fibres that are very strong when pulled.

104311.q: Which property does collagen give to bone?
104311.e: Collagen fibres work a bit like steel cables in concrete. They absorb pulling and bending forces so the bone doesn’t shatter so easily.
104311.m: Collagen makes bone tough and strong when pulled.

104312.q: What happens to a chicken bone left in vinegar for a few days?
104312.e: The acid dissolves the calcium minerals. What remains is the collagen framework, which can be bent.
104312.m: Without minerals, a bone is bendy like rubber.

104313.q: What happens to a bone that is strongly heated and burnt out?
a: It becomes brittle and crumbles easily
104313.e: The heat destroys the collagen. Only the minerals are left, which are hard but brittle.
104313.m: Without collagen, a bone becomes brittle.

104314.q: What is special about collagen among the proteins in the human body?
a: It is the most common protein
It is only found in blood
104314.e: About a quarter to a third of all proteins in the body is collagen. It is in bones, tendons, skin and cartilage.
104314.m: Collagen is the most common protein in the body.

104315.q: Which vitamin does the body need to build collagen properly?
104315.e: Without vitamin C, collagen is formed badly. That is why sailors used to suffer from scurvy, with bleeding gums and wounds that healed poorly.
104315.m: For healthy collagen you need vitamin C.

104316.q: Which food product is made from collagen?
104316.e: Gelatine is made by boiling skin and bones. The collagen is changed into a form that sets into a jelly when it cools.

104317.q: Apart from bone, in which tissue is collagen also the main ingredient?
104317.e: Tendons are mostly made of collagen fibres lying side by side. That way they can pass large pulling forces from muscles to bones.
104317.m: Thanks to collagen, tendons are extremely strong.

104318.q: What forms at the break in the first hours after a bone fracture?
104318.e: Blood flows from damaged vessels into the gap of the fracture. This haematoma is the starting point of healing.
104318.m: The healing of a fracture starts with a blood clot.

104319.q: What grows between the broken ends so that a bone heals?
104319.e: New tissue forms between the broken ends and bridges the gap. Bit by bit it turns into solid bone.
104319.m: New tissue joins the broken ends.

104320.q: What is the new tissue at a fracture like at first?
104320.e: At first, soft tissue made of connective tissue and cartilage forms. Later minerals are added and it becomes hard bone.
104320.m: At first the new tissue is soft; later it becomes hard.

104321.q: About how long does a simple fracture of a forearm bone take in adults until it can bear weight?
104321.e: Many simple fractures take about 6 to 8 weeks until the bone can bear weight again. Full remodelling often takes months.
104321.m: A broken bone takes several weeks to heal.

104322.q: Why is a broken bone often kept still with a cast or a splint?
a: So the broken ends grow together properly
So you can see it better
104322.e: If the broken ends keep moving, the callus can’t become firm. Keeping it still holds them in the right position.
104322.m: Keeping it still helps the bone grow back straight.

104323.q: What does a surgeon often use to join the broken pieces in an operation?
104323.e: In osteosynthesis, the pieces of bone are fixed with implants. That way they can heal in the right position.
104323.m: Plates and screws hold broken bones together.

104324.q: Who usually heals a broken bone faster?
104324.e: Children’s bones have a good blood supply and an active outer bone layer. That is why their fractures usually heal much faster.
104324.m: Bones heal especially fast in children.

104325.q: Why is an open fracture especially dangerous for healing?
a: Germs can get into the wound and the bone
The bone can no longer grow
The bone becomes soft at once
104325.e: With an open fracture, the skin over the break is injured. Bacteria can get in and cause a bone infection that greatly delays healing.
104325.m: Open fractures must be treated quickly because of the risk of infection.

104326.q: Which mineral is laid down in the new bone during healing?
104326.e: Bone-forming cells lay calcium into the new tissue. That makes the break hard and stable again.

104327.q: Who mainly gets a greenstick fracture?
104327.e: Children’s bones are bendier than adults’. That is why they often don’t break all the way through but buckle instead.
104327.m: Greenstick fractures are typical children’s fractures.

104328.q: Where does the greenstick fracture get its name from?
a: From a young branch that only breaks on one side when bent
From the green colour of the cast
104328.e: A fresh green twig splinters on one side when you bend it but doesn’t break right through. This type of fracture looks just like that.
104328.m: A greenstick fracture breaks like a fresh twig.

104329.q: What typically stays undamaged in a greenstick fracture?
104329.e: Children’s strong periosteum stays intact like a tube. It holds the broken pieces together.
104329.m: In a greenstick fracture, the periosteum holds the bone together.

104330.q: Why are children’s bones bendier than adults’?
a: They contain more collagen and fewer minerals
They are made entirely of cartilage
They are hollow with no wall
104330.e: Compared with minerals, children’s bones contain more elastic collagen. That is why they bend further before they break.
104330.m: Children’s bones are more elastic than adults’ bones.

104331.q: Where does a greenstick fracture happen especially often?
104331.e: When a child falls onto an outstretched hand, the ulna and radius bend a lot. Greenstick fractures often happen then.
104331.m: Falling on your hand often leads to a greenstick fracture of the forearm.

104332.q: How does a doctor reliably diagnose a greenstick fracture?
104332.e: An X-ray shows whether and how the bone is broken or bent. From the outside, a greenstick fracture is often hard to spot.
104332.m: An X-ray shows whether a bone is broken.

104333.q: Why do fractures usually heal faster in children than in adults?
a: Children’s bones are still growing and make new bone quickly
Children have twice as much blood
Children’s bones are made entirely of cartilage
104333.e: In children the bone is still growing and has a good blood supply. That is why new bone forms quickly at the break.
104333.m: Children’s bones heal faster than adults’ bones.

104334.q: How is a greenstick fracture that hasn’t moved out of place usually treated?
a: With a cast for a few weeks
104334.e: Because the periosteum is intact and the pieces have hardly moved, a cast is usually enough. Badly bent bones are straightened first.
104334.m: Greenstick fractures usually heal well in a cast.

104335.q: Which of these bones is a typical long bone?
104335.e: Long bones are long and have a hollow shaft. The tibia is a long bone of the lower leg.
104335.m: The long bones in the arms and legs are tubular long bones.

104336.q: What is the long middle part of a long bone called?
104336.e: The long, hollow middle part is called the shaft, or diaphysis in technical language. The marrow cavity is inside it.
104336.m: The middle part of a long bone is called the shaft.

104337.q: What covers the ends of a long bone in a joint?
104337.e: The thickened ends form the joint ends. Smooth cartilage covers them so the bones glide well in the joint.
104337.m: Cartilage covers the joint ends of bones.

104338.q: What is inside the shaft of a long bone?
a: An air space like in birds
104338.e: The shaft is hollow. The bone marrow lies in this marrow cavity, well protected by the firm wall of bone.
104338.m: The marrow cavity is inside the shaft of a long bone.

104339.q: What is the outer layer of the shaft of a long bone like?
104339.e: On the outside, bone has a firm outer layer called compact bone. In the shaft it is especially thick and carries heavy loads.
104339.m: The outer layer of bone is dense and hard.

104340.q: How is the bone tissue in the ends of long bones built?
a: Like a sponge, from fine struts of bone
104340.e: The fine struts of bone run along the lines of stress. That makes the bone light and still stable. Experts call this spongy bone.
104340.m: The ends of bones contain a fine framework of bony struts.

104341.q: What is the advantage of being built as a hollow tube?
a: The bone is light but still hard to bend
104341.e: For the same weight, a tube is much harder to bend than a thin solid rod. That is why bike frames are made of tubes too.
104341.m: Tubes are light and strong at the same time.

104342.q: Which bones of the hand count as short tubular bones?
104342.e: The finger bones and metacarpals have a shaft and two ends like long bones, but they are short. The wrist bones, on the other hand, are short, cube-like bones.
104342.m: The finger bones are small tubular bones too.

104343.q: Which of these bones is a flat bone?
104343.e: Flat bones are flat and wide. They include the shoulder blade, the breastbone and the bones of the top of the skull.
104343.m: The shoulder blade is a flat bone.

104344.q: What is the main job of the flat bones of the top of the skull?
104344.e: The curved plates of the top of the skull form a solid capsule around the delicate brain.
104344.m: The top of the skull protects the brain like a helmet.

104345.q: What is the advantage of the large surface of the shoulder blade?
a: Many muscles can attach to it
It makes especially lots of fatty marrow
104345.e: Many shoulder and back muscles attach to the wide surface of the shoulder blade. They move and stabilise the arm.
104345.m: Flat bones give muscles large areas to attach to.

104346.q: Which flat bone lies at the front in the middle of the chest?
104346.e: The breastbone is a flat bone. Most ribs are attached to it at the front.
104346.m: The breastbone lies at the front in the middle of the chest.

104347.q: How are the bones of the top of the skull built?
a: Two solid layers with spongy bone in between
As a hollow tube with a marrow cavity
From a single layer of fat
104347.e: An outer and an inner layer of solid compact bone enclose a layer of spongy bone. This design is light and stable.
104347.m: Flat bones are built like a sandwich.

104348.q: Apart from the skull and rib cage, where do you find large flat bones?
104348.e: The pelvis has wide, flat parts of bone that you can feel at the side of your hip. Fingers, toes and thighs, on the other hand, have long bones.
104348.m: The pelvis has wide flat bones too.

104349.q: Which of these bones is not a flat bone?
104349.e: The heel bone is a short, compact bone of the tarsus. The parietal bone, breastbone and ribs count as flat bones.
104349.m: Not every bone is flat; the heel bone is a short bone.

104350.q: Which flat bones form the rib cage together with the spine?
104350.e: Together with the thoracic spine, the ribs and breastbone enclose the heart and lungs.
104350.m: Ribs and breastbone form a protective cage.

104351.q: Which deficiency is the most common cause of rickets?
104351.e: Without enough vitamin D, the body can put too little calcium into the bones. The bones stay soft and bend out of shape.
104351.m: Rickets is usually caused by too little vitamin D.

104352.q: How does the body make vitamin D itself?
104352.e: The sun’s UVB rays trigger the production of vitamin D in the skin. In winter the sun in Switzerland is often not strong enough for this.
104352.m: Sunlight helps the skin make vitamin D.

104353.q: Which typical feature do children with severe rickets show in their legs?
104353.e: The soft bones bend under the body’s weight. That often causes bow legs or knock knees.
104353.m: Soft bones bend into bow legs.

104354.q: What used to be given to children against rickets?
104354.e: Cod liver oil is an oil from fish liver and contains a lot of vitamin D. Many children used to have to swallow a spoonful every day.
104354.m: Cod liver oil contains a lot of vitamin D.

104355.q: What is recommended for babies in Switzerland to prevent rickets?
a: An hour of sunbathing every day
A glass of cow’s milk a day
104355.e: In Switzerland it is recommended to give babies and toddlers vitamin D drops every day during their first years of life.
104355.m: Babies in Switzerland are given vitamin D drops as a precaution.

104356.q: Why does the body need vitamin D for healthy bones?
a: It helps calcium to be absorbed from the gut
104356.e: Vitamin D makes sure enough calcium and phosphate from food get into the blood. These minerals harden the bones.
104356.m: Vitamin D helps absorb calcium for the bones.

104357.q: Which food contains a lot of vitamin D?
104357.e: Oily fish such as salmon, herring or mackerel are among the best sources of vitamin D. Fruit, vegetables and grains contain hardly any vitamin D.
104357.m: Oily fish provides a lot of vitamin D.

104358.e: In children the bones are still growing. If vitamin D is missing, the growing bones don’t get hard enough and bend.

104359.q: Why was rickets especially common in industrial cities in the 19th century?
a: Smoke and narrow streets kept out the sunlight
The children drank too much water
The children moved around too much
104359.e: In smoky cities with dark homes, children hardly got any sun. Without sunlight their skin made too little vitamin D.
104359.m: Little sunlight used to encourage rickets.

104360.q: Which method is usually used to measure bone density?
104360.e: In a bone density scan, called DXA, weak X-rays are used to find out how many minerals the bone contains.
104360.m: Bone density is measured with weak X-rays.

104361.q: What is the disease called in which bone density drops sharply?
104361.e: With osteoporosis, bones lose mass and become porous. They then break even in minor falls.

104362.q: Which kind of sport especially strengthens bone density?
104362.e: Impacts and loads stimulate the bone-forming cells. In swimming or cycling the bones are loaded less.
104362.m: Jumping and running make bones strong.

104363.q: Why do astronauts’ bones weaken in space?
a: The load from gravity is missing
It is too cold in space
They are not allowed to eat calcium
104363.e: Bones need loading to stay strong. In weightlessness it is missing, so space travellers lose bone mass despite training.

104364.q: At about what age do people reach their highest bone density?
104364.e: Until about the age of 30, more bone is built than broken down. Anyone who builds up lots of bone mass when young has a bigger reserve later.
104364.m: Bone density is highest around the age of 30.

104365.q: What share of the body’s calcium is in the bones and teeth?
104365.e: Almost all of the body’s calcium is stored in the bones and teeth. Only a small remainder is in the blood and the cells.
104365.m: The bones are the body’s big calcium store.

104366.q: Which habit is proven to harm bone density?
104366.e: Smoking disturbs bone building and increases the risk of osteoporosis. Exercise that puts load on the bones, on the other hand, strengthens them.

104367.q: What happens to our bones throughout our lives?
a: They are constantly broken down and rebuilt
104367.e: Special cells break down old bone, and others build new bone. That way the skeleton constantly renews itself.

104368.q: Which fracture is especially feared in older people with osteoporosis?
104368.e: After a fall, the neck of the thighbone often breaks in porous bones. That usually means an operation and a long recovery.
104368.m: With osteoporosis, the neck of the thighbone often breaks.

104469.q: What is the flat, usually green main part of a leaf called?
104469.e: The leaf blade is the actual surface of the leaf. It is usually thin and broad.
104469.m: The leaf blade is the flat main part of the leaf.

104470.q: Why is the leaf blade flat and broad in most plants?
a: That way it catches lots of light
That way it can store rain
That way it becomes poisonous to animals
That way it holds the roots in place
104470.e: A large, flat surface takes in a lot of sunlight. The plant needs this light for photosynthesis.
104470.m: A broad leaf surface catches lots of light for photosynthesis.

104471.q: Which three main parts does a typical leaf consist of?
a: Leaf base, leaf stalk, leaf blade
104471.e: The leaf is attached to the shoot by the leaf base, and the leaf stalk carries the blade. The blade is the actual surface of the leaf.
104471.m: A leaf consists of the leaf base, leaf stalk and leaf blade.

104472.q: What is the end of the leaf blade furthest from the stalk called?
104472.e: The leaf tip is at the outer end of the blade. At the other end, by the stalk, is the leaf base.
104472.m: The leaf tip is the outer end of the leaf blade.

104473.q: Which water plant from South America has round floating leaves more than 2 m across?
104473.e: The giant water lily (Victoria) from the Amazon region has huge, round leaf blades with an upturned edge. They are among the largest undivided leaves in the world.
104473.m: The giant water lily has floating leaves more than two metres across.

104474.q: Why are shade leaves usually larger and thinner than sun leaves on the same plant?
a: They catch more of the weak light
104474.e: There is little light in the shade. A large, thin leaf blade makes the best use of the little light with little material.
104474.m: Shade leaves are large and thin to make good use of little light.

104475.q: What do you call a leaf whose blade is not divided into separate leaflets, as in the beech?
104475.e: In a simple leaf the blade forms one continuous surface. If it is split into separate leaflets, it is called a compound leaf.
104475.m: A simple leaf has an undivided leaf blade.

104476.q: What is the long, drawn-out leaf tip of many rainforest plants called, which lets rainwater run off quickly?
104476.e: The drip tip carries rainwater quickly away from the leaf blade. This way the leaf does not stay wet for long in the damp rainforest, and algae and fungi grow less well on it.
104476.m: The drip tip lets rainwater drip off the leaf quickly.

104477.q: Besides holding up the leaf blade, what job does the leaf stalk do?
a: It carries substances between leaf and shoot
It takes water from the soil
104477.e: The transport tubes that connect the leaf to the shoot run through the leaf stalk. Without them the leaf blade would be cut off from its supply.
104477.m: Substances flow between leaf and shoot through the leaf stalk.

104478.q: What do you call a leaf without a stalk that is attached directly to the stem?
104478.e: When there is no leaf stalk, the blade sits directly on the shoot. Such leaves are called sessile.
104478.m: A sessile leaf has no leaf stalk.

104479.q: Why do the leaves of the aspen move even in a light wind?
a: Its leaf stalk is flattened sideways
Its leaf blade is filled with air
104479.e: The flattened leaf stalk bends easily from side to side. So the leaves of the aspen tremble in the slightest breeze.
104479.m: The aspen trembles because of its flat leaf stalks.

104480.q: In which garden plant do you mainly eat the thick leaf stalks?
104480.e: The red or green sticks of rhubarb are leaf stalks. The large leaf blades are not eaten because they contain a lot of oxalic acid.
104480.m: With rhubarb you eat the leaf stalks.

104481.q: What is the angle between the leaf stalk and the shoot called, where a bud often sits?
104481.e: The leaf axil lies between the upper side of the leaf stalk and the stem. A side bud often forms there.
104481.m: A bud often sits in the leaf axil.

104482.q: How does the leaf stalk help the plant get as much light as possible?
a: It turns the leaf blade towards the light
104482.e: The leaf stalk can bend and twist as it grows. In this way it moves the leaf blade into a good position for the light.
104482.m: The leaf stalk turns the leaf blade towards the light.

104483.q: What are the small, leaf-like outgrowths at the base of the leaf stalk called, for example in the rose?
104483.e: Stipules grow at the base of the leaf. In the pea they are especially large and help with photosynthesis.
104483.m: Stipules sit at the base of the leaf stalk.

104484.q: What is the part of the leaf called that wraps around the stem of grasses like a tube?
104484.e: Grasses usually have no proper leaf stalk. The base of the leaf has turned into a leaf sheath that wraps around and supports the stem.
104484.m: In grasses the leaf sheath wraps around the stem.

104485.q: What is the strong vein called that runs down the middle of the blade in many leaves?
104485.e: The midrib is the main vein of the leaf. The side veins branch off from it.
104485.m: The midrib is the main vein of the leaf.

104486.q: What do the leaf veins carry out of the leaf into the rest of the plant?
104486.e: The leaf veins bring water and minerals into the leaf. They carry the sugar made there to the roots, fruits and other parts.
104486.m: Leaf veins carry sugar from the leaf to the whole plant.

104487.q: Which plant has leaves with veins that run parallel?
104487.e: Maize is a monocot. In monocots the leaf veins usually run parallel from the base of the leaf to the tip.
104487.m: Monocots such as maize usually have parallel leaf veins.

104488.q: Which vein pattern is typical of the leaves of broadleaved trees such as beech or lime?
104488.e: In dicots the veins branch into a fine network. You can see this net pattern well if you hold a leaf up to the light.
104488.m: Broadleaved trees usually have net-like branching leaf veins.

104489.q: What do the leaf veins carry from the plant into the leaf?
104489.e: Water with dissolved minerals rises from the roots through the stem into the leaf veins. In the leaf the plant needs it for photosynthesis.
104489.m: Leaf veins bring water into the leaf.

104490.q: What do you see if you stand a pale stem with leaves, such as celery, in water with ink for a few hours?
a: The leaves fall off at once
104490.e: The coloured water rises in fine tubes up into the leaves. This shows that the leaf veins carry water.
104490.m: Water flows through the leaf veins into the leaves.

104491.q: Apart from transporting substances, what job do the leaf veins have?
104491.e: The veins act like a framework and keep the thin blade spread out. You can see this well in skeleton leaves, where only the veins are left.
104491.m: Leaf veins support the leaf like a framework.

104492.q: Which tree has fan-shaped leaves whose veins keep splitting into forks?
104492.e: The leaf veins of the ginkgo branch in forks without forming a network. This is a very ancient form of vein pattern.
104492.m: The ginkgo has fork-branched leaf veins.

104493.q: What is left of a skeleton leaf once the soft leaf tissue has rotted away?
104493.e: The leaf veins are tougher than the rest of the leaf tissue. When the soft tissue rots, a fine network of veins is left behind.
104493.m: A skeleton leaf consists only of the leaf veins.

104494.q: What is the outermost layer of cells on the upper and lower side of a leaf called?
104494.e: The epidermis is the outer covering layer of the leaf. It protects the inside of the leaf from injury and germs.
104494.m: The epidermis is the outer skin layer of the leaf.

104495.q: Why are most cells of the leaf epidermis see-through?
a: Light needs to reach the inside of the leaf
104495.e: The epidermis works like a clear window. This lets light reach the green cells inside, where photosynthesis takes place.
104495.m: The see-through epidermis lets light into the leaf.

104496.q: How many layers of cells make up the epidermis in most leaves?
104496.e: The epidermis is usually only a single layer of cells thick. It is still strong because the cells fit together without gaps.
104496.m: The epidermis usually consists of a single layer of cells.

104497.q: How many guard cells together form one stoma?
104497.e: A stoma consists of two guard cells with a gap between them. Under the microscope they look like two beans.
104497.m: A stoma is formed by two guard cells.

104498.q: What do guard cells have, unlike the other cells of the epidermis?
104498.e: The ordinary epidermis cells are colourless. The guard cells, however, contain chloroplasts.

104499.q: On which side of its leaves does the water lily have its stomata?
104499.e: Water lily leaves lie with their underside on the water. That is why the stomata are on top, where they are in contact with the air.
104499.m: The water lily has its stomata on the upper side of the leaf.

104500.q: What is the release of water vapour through the leaves called?
104500.e: Water evaporates from the leaf through the stomata. This transpiration pulls new water up from the roots.
104500.m: Plants release water vapour during transpiration.

104501.q: From which layer of cells do the stinging hairs of the nettle grow?
104501.e: Leaf hairs, including stinging hairs, are outgrowths of the epidermis. When touched, their tip breaks off and the stinging juice gets into the skin.
104501.m: Stinging hairs are outgrowths of the epidermis.

104502.q: What is the layer of long, tightly packed cells just below the upper epidermis called?
104502.e: In the palisade tissue, slim cells stand close together. It lies just below the upper epidermis, where most light arrives.
104502.m: The palisade tissue lies directly below the upper epidermis.

104503.q: Why is palisade tissue called that?
a: Its cells stand like fence posts
It is as hard as a plank
104503.e: A palisade is a fence made of closely set posts. The long cells stand upright next to each other in just the same way.
104503.m: The cells of the palisade tissue stand like the posts of a fence.

104504.q: In which tissue of a leaf does most photosynthesis take place?
104504.e: The palisade cells lie directly below the upper epidermis, where most light arrives. That is why most photosynthesis happens there.
104504.m: Most photosynthesis takes place in the palisade tissue.

104505.q: What do the cells of the palisade tissue contain especially many of?
104505.e: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts. Photosynthesis takes place in these green parts of the cell.
104505.m: Palisade cells are full of chloroplasts.

104506.q: How can you recognise a sun leaf in cross-section under the microscope?
104506.e: Sun leaves often have several layers of palisade cells. This lets them make better use of strong light, and they are thicker than shade leaves.
104506.m: Sun leaves have a thick palisade tissue.

104507.q: Which tissue lies below the palisade tissue in a leaf and has many air spaces?
104507.e: The spongy tissue consists of loosely arranged cells with many air spaces. Gases reach the cells and the stomata through them.
104507.m: Below the palisade tissue lies the loose spongy tissue.

104508.q: How are the cells of the palisade tissue lined up in relation to the leaf surface?
104508.e: The long palisade cells stand upright to the surface. This way many cells with many chloroplasts fit under the lit area.
104508.m: Palisade cells stand upright to the leaf surface.

104509.q: Why is the upper side of many leaves darker green than the underside?
a: The palisade tissue lies beneath it
104509.e: The dense, green palisade tissue lies below the upper epidermis. That is why the upper side looks darker than the underside.
104509.m: The upper side of a leaf is darker because the palisade tissue lies there.

104510.q: If you put a leaf in hot water, small air bubbles rise from its underside. Where does this air come from?
a: from the sugar in the leaf
104510.e: The heat makes the air in the spaces inside the leaf expand. It escapes through the stomata, which in most leaves are on the underside.
104510.m: A leaf contains air inside that can escape through the stomata.

104511.q: What is typical of the spongy tissue of a leaf?
a: tightly packed cells with no gaps
104511.e: The cells of the spongy tissue are irregularly shaped and loosely arranged. Between them are many air-filled spaces.
104511.m: The spongy tissue is loosely built and full of air spaces.

104512.q: What are the air spaces in the spongy tissue for?
a: for gas exchange in the leaf
for holding on to the twig
104512.e: The carbon dioxide that comes in through the stomata spreads out in the air spaces. Oxygen and water vapour leave the same way.
104512.m: The air spaces in the spongy tissue are used for gas exchange.

104513.q: ‘Inter’ means ‘between’. So what are the intercellular spaces in the spongy tissue?
a: Cells with extra lots of chlorophyll
104513.e: Intercellular means ‘between the cells’. These air-filled spaces form a connected air system in the leaf.
104513.m: Intercellular spaces are air spaces between the cells.

104514.q: Through which openings does air from outside get into the spongy tissue of a leaf?
104514.e: The stomata are usually on the underside of the leaf. Air flows through them into the spaces of the spongy tissue.
104514.m: Air gets into the inside of the leaf through the stomata.

104515.q: Do the cells of the spongy tissue contain chloroplasts?
a: Yes, but fewer than palisade cells
104515.e: Photosynthesis also takes place in the spongy tissue. But its cells have fewer chloroplasts than the palisade cells.
104515.m: Spongy tissue has fewer chloroplasts than palisade tissue.

104516.q: Why can the large leaves of the water lily float on the water?
a: Their leaf tissue has large air spaces
They are held up by the stalk
104516.e: The tissue of floating leaves has especially large, air-filled spaces. They give the leaf buoyancy.
104516.m: Floating leaves have large air spaces inside them.

104517.q: In which order are the layers of a leaf arranged from top to bottom?
a: Palisade tissue, epidermis, spongy tissue, cuticle
Spongy tissue, epidermis, palisade tissue, epidermis
104517.e: At the top is the epidermis with the cuticle, below it the palisade tissue. Then come the spongy tissue and the lower epidermis.
104517.m: Below the upper epidermis come the palisade tissue, spongy tissue and lower epidermis.

104518.q: What is the waxy protective layer on the epidermis of a leaf called?
104518.e: The cuticle covers the outside of the epidermis like a thin film. It repels water.
104518.m: The cuticle is a waxy layer on the leaf.

104519.q: What is the most important job of the cuticle?
104519.e: The waxy cuticle hardly lets any water through. So only a little water evaporates over the leaf surface, apart from through the stomata.
104519.m: The cuticle protects the leaf from drying out.

104520.e: The cells of the epidermis release the substances of the cuticle to the outside. This forms a closed layer over the leaf.
104520.m: The epidermis cells make the cuticle.

104521.q: Which everyday substance is the cuticle of a leaf most like?
104521.e: The cuticle is made mainly of waxy substances. Like a candle, it repels water.
104521.m: The cuticle is waxy and repels water.

104522.q: Why are the leaves of ivy and holly shiny?
104522.e: A thick, smooth cuticle reflects light like a coat of varnish. Ivy and holly are also evergreen.
104522.m: A thick cuticle makes leaves shiny.

104523.q: Which plants usually have an especially thick cuticle?
104523.e: Where there is little water, a plant has to be thrifty. That is why cacti and many desert plants have a thick cuticle.
104523.m: Plants of dry places have a thick cuticle.

104524.q: What is the effect called when water rolls off some leaves and takes dirt with it?
104524.e: Tiny wax bumps on the leaf surface make water form drops. The drops roll off and take dirt with them.
104524.m: With the lotus effect, water rolls off and cleans the leaf.

104525.q: Why does the cuticle not get in the way of photosynthesis?
a: It falls off during the day
104525.e: The cuticle is a thin, translucent layer. So sunlight gets into the inside of the leaf unhindered.
104525.m: The see-through cuticle lets light through.

104526.q: What shape is the leaf of the silver birch?
104526.e: The birch leaf is triangular to diamond-shaped and has a double-toothed edge. It is small and thin.
104526.m: The silver birch has diamond-shaped leaves.

104527.q: Which tree has hand-shaped, lobed leaves like the one on Canada’s flag?
104527.e: The maple leaf has several pointed lobes that stick out like the fingers of a hand. A maple leaf is the symbol of Canada.

104528.q: What do you call a roundish leaf shape with a deep notch at the stalk, as in asarabacca?
104528.e: Kidney-shaped leaves are usually wider than they are long and have a deep notch where the stalk joins. So the blade looks like a kidney.

104529.q: What do you call a long, narrow leaf shape with a point, as in the white willow?
104529.e: Lance-shaped leaves are much longer than they are wide and taper to a point like a lance. They are typical of many willows.

104530.q: What shape is the leaf of the common beech?
104530.e: The beech leaf is egg-shaped to oval and has a short point at the front. It is about 5 to 10 cm long.
104530.m: The common beech has egg-shaped leaves.

104531.q: What do you call the long, narrow leaf shape of grasses, with almost parallel edges?
104531.e: Strap-shaped leaves are narrow and their edges run almost parallel. Most grass leaves look like this.

104532.q: What leaf shape does the nasturtium have, whose stalk joins in the middle of the round blade?
104532.e: In shield-shaped leaves the stalk is not attached at the edge but under the middle of the blade. The leaf then looks like a small shield.

104533.q: What leaf shape does the English oak have?
104533.e: The oak leaf has several rounded lobes with deep bays between them. This makes the oak very easy to recognise.
104533.m: Oak leaves have wavy, rounded lobes.

104534.q: What do you call a smooth leaf edge with no teeth or cuts?
104534.e: An entire leaf has a smooth edge. Examples are lilac and ivy on flowering shoots.
104534.m: An entire leaf has a smooth edge.

104535.q: What do you call a leaf edge with sharp teeth pointing forwards?
104535.e: The teeth of a serrated leaf point towards the leaf tip, as on a saw. One example is the wild cherry.
104535.m: A serrated leaf edge has sharp teeth pointing forwards.

104536.q: What do you call a leaf edge with rounded teeth?
104536.e: On a crenate leaf edge the teeth are round and the notches pointed. Serrated edges, on the other hand, have pointed teeth.
104536.m: A crenate leaf edge has round teeth.

104537.q: Which tree has double-serrated leaves, where big teeth carry more small teeth?
104537.e: In the hornbeam the bigger teeth on the leaf edge carry smaller teeth again. This edge is called double-serrated.

104538.q: Which native plant has spiny, toothed leaf edges, especially on young plants?
104538.e: The leaves of holly have hard, prickly teeth along the edge. They protect against animals that want to eat the leaves.

104539.q: Which tree has long, narrow leaves with a coarsely toothed edge and a fine point on each tooth, and often grows in Ticino?
104539.e: The sweet chestnut has leaves more than 20 cm long with bristle-tipped teeth. On the southern side of the Alps it forms large chestnut forests.
104539.m: The sweet chestnut has long leaves with sharply toothed edges.

104540.q: What leaf edge does the common beech have?
104540.e: The edge of the beech leaf is smooth and slightly wavy. Young leaves also have fine hairs along the edge.
104540.m: The common beech has a smooth, slightly wavy leaf edge.

104541.q: Why do people look at the leaf edge when identifying trees?
a: It is typical of many species
It shows the type of soil
104541.e: Whether a leaf is smooth, serrated or crenate tells many species apart. Together with leaf shape and leaf arrangement, the edge helps with identification.
104541.m: The leaf edge helps to identify plants.

104542.q: What leaf edge does the stinging nettle have?
104542.e: The leaves of the stinging nettle have coarse, pointed teeth along the edge. Together with the stinging hairs, this makes it easy to recognise.
104542.m: The stinging nettle has coarsely serrated leaves.

a: Leaflets on a shared central stalk
104543.e: In a pinnate leaf several leaflets sit left and right on a central stalk. The whole thing is one single leaf.
104543.m: A pinnate leaf consists of leaflets on a central stalk.

104544.q: Which native tree has pinnate leaves?
104544.e: The common ash has long pinnate leaves with many leaflets. Beech, lime and hornbeam have simple leaves.

104545.q: What do you call a pinnate leaf with a single leaflet at the tip?
104545.e: Odd-pinnate leaves end with a single leaflet, so the number of leaflets is odd. Examples are the rose and the walnut.
104545.m: Odd-pinnate leaves have a leaflet at the tip.

104546.q: What do the top leaflets of the pea turn into?
104546.e: In the pea the end leaflets have turned into tendrils. With them the plant climbs up supports.
104546.m: The pea holds on with leaflets that have turned into tendrils.

104547.q: What is a leaf called whose leaflets all start from one point like the fingers of a hand?
104547.e: In palmate leaves all the leaflets start at the tip of the stalk. The horse chestnut has such leaves.
104547.m: The horse chestnut has palmate leaves.

104548.q: How can you tell that a pinnate leaf is a single leaf and not a twig?
a: A bud sits only at its base
It is always shorter than 5 cm
104548.e: Buds only form at the base of a whole leaf, where it joins the twig. You find no buds at the individual leaflets.
104548.m: Only at the base of a pinnate leaf is there a bud.

104549.q: Which tree with pinnate leaves has bright red berries in autumn that birds love to eat?
104549.e: The rowan or mountain ash has odd-pinnate leaves. Its red fruits are an important food for birds.
104549.m: The rowan has pinnate leaves and red berries.

104550.q: How are the leaflets arranged on a pinnate leaf?
a: Left and right on a shared central stalk
All at one single point like fingers
Stacked on top of each other like a tower
104550.e: In a pinnate leaf the leaflets sit in pairs on a central stalk, rather like the branches of a feather. If they all start from one point, the leaf is called palmate.
104550.m: Pinnate leaves have their leaflets left and right on a central stalk.

104551.q: From a botanical point of view, what is a conifer needle?
104551.e: Needles are modified leaves. Like broad leaves, they have an epidermis, stomata and green tissue for photosynthesis.
104551.m: A needle is a narrow leaf.

104552.q: How can you recognise the needles of the silver fir by their underside?
104552.e: Two whitish wax stripes run along the underside of the fir needle. The stomata are there.
104552.m: Silver fir needles have two white stripes underneath.

104553.q: What shape is the cross-section of a spruce needle?
104553.e: Spruce needles are four-sided and can be rolled between your fingers. Fir needles, on the other hand, are flat.

104554.q: How long does a spruce needle normally stay on the tree?
104554.e: Spruce needles stay on the twig for several years before they fall. Because they never all fall at once, the spruce is evergreen.
104554.m: Spruce needles stay on the tree for several years.

104555.q: Which native conifer has soft, flat needles and is poisonous in almost all its parts?
104555.e: The yew has dark green, soft needles. Needles and seeds are very poisonous; only the red seed coat is not poisonous.
104555.m: The yew is poisonous and has soft needles.

104556.q: In which conifer do the prickly needles usually grow in groups of three in a whorl?
104556.e: In the common juniper three pointed needles grow at each spot on the twig. Its blue-black berry cones are used as a spice.
104556.m: Juniper has its needles in threes.

104557.q: Why do needles lose only a little water even in winter?
a: They are narrow and coated with wax
They take in water from the air
104557.e: Needles have a small surface and a thick layer of wax. So little water evaporates, even when the ground is frozen.
104557.m: Narrow, waxy needles protect against water loss.

104558.q: How are the needles of the silver fir arranged on most twigs?
a: all round like a bottle brush
only at the tip of the twig
104558.e: Fir needles usually stick out sideways in two rows, like parted hair. In the spruce, on the other hand, they stand all round the twig.
104558.m: Fir needles are parted on the twig.

104559.q: What do you call the leaf arrangement where only one leaf grows at each node?
104559.e: In an alternate arrangement only one leaf grows at each node. The leaves point to different sides in turn, as in the beech.
104559.m: Alternate leaves grow singly at each node.

104560.q: What do you call the leaf arrangement where two leaves sit exactly opposite each other at the same node?
104560.e: Opposite leaves stand in pairs facing each other. One example is lilac.
104560.m: Opposite leaves stand in pairs facing each other.

104561.q: What is it called when each pair of leaves is turned at a right angle to the one before?
104561.e: In a decussate arrangement each pair of leaves is turned 90 degrees to the previous one. This is typical of the mint family, such as peppermint.
104561.m: Decussate leaf pairs are each turned by 90 degrees.

104562.q: What do you call the leaf arrangement where three or more leaves sit at one node?
104562.e: In whorled plants several leaves form a ring around the stem. A well-known example is sweet woodruff.
104562.m: Whorled leaves form a ring around the stem.

104563.q: What is the arrangement called where all the leaves lie close to the ground in a circle, as in the dandelion?
104563.e: In a leaf rosette all the leaves start close together at the base of the plant. So they lie flat on the ground.
104563.m: The dandelion forms a leaf rosette.

104564.q: What is the advantage of leaves on a shoot being offset from each other?
104564.e: Offset leaves do not lie exactly on top of each other. This way each leaf gets as much light as possible.
104564.m: Offset leaves shade each other very little.

104565.q: What leaf arrangement does the stinging nettle have?
104565.e: In the stinging nettle the leaves stand in pairs opposite each other. Each pair is turned at a right angle to the one before.
104565.m: The stinging nettle has decussate leaves.

104566.q: What is it called when a plant’s leaves fill the gaps between them so that they hardly overlap?
104566.e: In a leaf mosaic the leaves, with stalks of different lengths, arrange themselves so that they fit together like jigsaw pieces. You can see this well in ivy on a wall, for example.
104566.m: In a leaf mosaic the leaves fill the gaps.

104567.q: How can you tell a maple from a plane tree on the twig, when their leaves look similar?
104567.e: Maple leaves stand in pairs opposite each other. In the plane tree only one leaf grows at each node.
104567.m: Maple leaves are opposite, plane leaves alternate.

104667.q: Where on the body is the triceps?
a: At the back of the upper arm
At the front of the upper arm
At the back of the thigh
At the front of the forearm
104667.e: The triceps (musculus triceps brachii) lies on the back of the upper arm.
104667.m: The triceps is at the back of the upper arm.

104668.q: Which movement does the triceps make at the elbow joint?
104668.e: When the triceps contracts, the forearm is straightened at the elbow.

104669.q: How many heads does the triceps have?
104669.e: The name comes from the Latin “tri” for three: the muscle has a long, a lateral and a medial head.

104670.q: Which muscle is the direct opponent of the triceps?
104670.e: The biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it. They work as opponents.
104670.m: The biceps and triceps are an opposing pair on the upper arm.

104671.q: What attaches the triceps to the bones?
104671.e: Muscles are connected to bones by tough tendons. The triceps tendon runs to the elbow and so straightens the arm.

104672.q: Which exercise works the triceps especially hard?
104672.e: When you push up from a press-up, the elbows straighten. This work is done mainly by the triceps.
104672.m: If you push yourself up with your arms, you need your triceps.

104673.q: What does the triceps do while the biceps bends the arm?
104673.e: The biceps and triceps are opponents. When one contracts, the other relaxes and is stretched.
104673.m: When the biceps bends, the triceps relaxes.

104674.q: What tells the triceps to contract?
104674.e: The brain sends signals through nerves to the muscles. Only then does the triceps contract and straighten the arm.

a: At the front of the thigh
At the back of the thigh
104675.e: The quadriceps (musculus quadriceps femoris) forms the powerful front of the thigh.
104675.m: The quadriceps forms the front of the thigh.

104676.q: How many heads does the quadriceps have?
104676.e: “Quadri” means four. The muscle is made of four parts that end together in one tendon.
104676.m: The quadriceps is made of four heads.

104677.q: What is the main job of the quadriceps?
104677.e: When the quadriceps contracts, the lower leg is straightened at the knee joint, for example when you stand up.
104677.m: The quadriceps straightens the leg at the knee.

104678.q: Which bone is embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps?
104678.e: The kneecap (patella) lies in the tendon of the quadriceps. It works like a pulley and protects the knee joint.
104678.m: The kneecap sits in the tendon of the quadriceps.

104679.q: Which exercise especially strengthens the quadriceps?
104679.e: In squats the quadriceps straightens the knee again and again against your body weight. Press-ups and pull-ups mainly train the arms and upper body.

104680.q: Which muscle group is the opponent of the quadriceps?
a: The hamstrings at the back of the thigh
104680.e: The muscles at the back of the thigh bend the knee and the quadriceps straightens it.
104680.m: At the front the quadriceps straightens; at the back the hamstrings bend.

104681.q: What happens when the tendon just below the kneecap is tapped lightly?
104681.e: In the knee-jerk reflex, the quadriceps is briefly stretched and then contracts by reflex. The lower leg kicks forwards.
104681.m: The knee-jerk reflex shows that the quadriceps responds to stretching.

104682.q: In which activity does the quadriceps work especially hard?
104682.e: When you climb stairs, the knee has to be straightened under your body weight. That is done by the quadriceps.
104682.m: Climbing stairs and cycling strengthen the quadriceps.

104683.q: Where on the body is the deltoid muscle?
a: It forms the rounded shape of the shoulder
It is in the back of the neck under the skull
104683.e: The deltoid lies like a cap over the shoulder joint. It gives the shoulder its round shape.
104683.m: The deltoid forms the rounded shape of the shoulder.

104684.q: Which joint does the deltoid cover like a cap?
104684.e: The deltoid wraps around the shoulder joint from the front, above and behind. That way it can move the arm in many directions.
104684.m: The deltoid sits like a cap over the shoulder joint.

104685.q: Which movement does the middle part of the deltoid mainly make?
a: Lifting the arm out to the side
Putting the arm behind the back
104685.e: The middle part lifts the arm sideways away from the body. Experts call this abduction.
104685.m: The deltoid lifts the arm to the side.

104686.q: Into which muscle is a vaccine often injected in teenagers and adults?
104686.e: Many vaccines are injected into the deltoid on the upper arm because it is easy to reach and has a good blood supply.
104686.m: Many vaccines go into the deltoid on the upper arm.

104687.q: Where does the deltoid muscle get its name from?
a: From its triangular shape like the Greek letter delta
From the Latin word for shoulder
104687.e: The muscle looks like a triangle standing on its point, similar to the Greek capital letter delta (Δ).
104687.m: The deltoid is triangular like the letter delta.

104688.q: Which bone is the deltoid attached to?
104688.e: Its fibres run down over the shoulder and come together, attaching roughly in the middle of the humerus.
104688.m: The deltoid runs from the shoulder to the humerus.

104689.q: Which exercise mainly trains the deltoid?
104689.e: When you press weights over your head, the shoulder lifts the arm. The deltoid works especially hard.

104690.q: What makes the deltoid contract when you want to lift your arm?
a: A nerve brings a signal from the brain
The heart presses on the muscle
The lungs blow air into the muscle
104690.e: The brain sends electrical signals through nerves to the muscles. For the deltoid it is the axillary nerve.
104690.m: Nerves carry the command from the brain to the muscle.

104691.q: What is an antagonist among muscles?
104691.e: An antagonist causes the opposite movement to another muscle: if one bends a joint, the other straightens it again.
104691.m: An antagonist is a muscle’s opponent.

104692.q: Why does a joint need muscles that work as opponents?
a: Muscles can only pull, not push
One muscle on its own would be too heavy
Otherwise there would be no blood
104692.e: A muscle can only shorten and so pull. To move back, a second muscle is needed on the other side.
104692.m: Muscles can only pull, so opponents are needed.

104693.q: What do you call the muscle that mainly carries out a movement?
104693.e: The agonist (player) carries out the movement, and the antagonist makes the opposite movement.
104693.m: The agonist is the player; the antagonist is the opponent.

104694.q: Which muscle bends the arm at the elbow?
104694.e: The biceps lies at the front of the upper arm and bends the elbow. Its opponent, the triceps, straightens the arm again.

104695.q: What does the antagonist do while the agonist contracts?
104695.e: For the movement to be smooth, the opponent lets go and is stretched.
104695.m: When the agonist pulls, the antagonist gives way.

104696.q: Which muscles of the trunk are the opponents of the back extensors?
104696.e: The tummy muscles bend the trunk forwards and the back extensors straighten it up again.
104696.m: Tummy muscles and back extensors are opponents in the trunk.

104697.q: In the biceps and triceps pair, what is stretched when you bend your elbow?
104697.e: When you bend, the biceps contracts. The triceps on the back relaxes and is stretched.
104697.m: When you bend your arm, the triceps is stretched.

104698.q: Why should you train both agonist and antagonist in strength training?
a: So the muscles stay in balance
So you need to drink less
104698.e: If one muscle is much stronger than its opponent, it can worsen your posture and put one-sided strain on joints.
104698.m: Train opposing muscles in a balanced way.

104699.e: Smooth muscles work by themselves, for example in the gut or in blood vessels. We can’t move them on purpose.
104699.m: Smooth muscles work without us wanting them to.

a: In the wall of the gut
104700.e: Smooth muscles lie in the walls of internal organs such as the stomach, gut and blood vessels.
104700.m: Smooth muscles are found in the walls of internal organs.

104701.q: What is the wave-like movement called with which smooth muscles push food through the gut?
104701.e: In peristalsis, the muscles of the gut wall contract one after another and push the contents along.
104701.m: Peristalsis pushes food through the gut.

104702.q: What do you feel when the smooth muscles in the gut cramp?
104702.e: The smooth muscles in the gut wall normally contract gently. If they cramp, you feel it as tummy cramps.
104702.m: Cramping gut muscles cause tummy cramps.

104704.q: What does the smooth muscle in the walls of blood vessels control?
104704.e: When the smooth muscles in the vessel wall contract, the vessel gets narrower. That helps control blood pressure.
104704.m: Smooth muscles make blood vessels narrower or wider.

104705.q: How does smooth muscle work compared with skeletal muscle?
a: More slowly, but with great endurance
Just as fast and just as tired
104705.e: Smooth muscles contract slowly but can hold the tension for a long time without getting tired.
104705.m: Smooth muscles are slow but have great endurance.

104706.q: Which part of the nervous system controls smooth muscle?
a: Only the spinal cord on its own
104706.e: The autonomic nervous system works by itself and controls organs such as the gut, blood vessels and airways.
104706.m: The autonomic nervous system controls the smooth muscles.

a: A blood vessel in the muscle
104707.e: In skeletal muscle, a single long muscle cell is called a muscle fibre.
104707.m: A muscle fibre is a single cell of skeletal muscle.

104708.q: How many nuclei does a skeletal muscle fibre have?
104708.e: A muscle fibre forms from many fused precursor cells and so has many nuclei.
104708.m: Skeletal muscle fibres have many nuclei.

104709.q: What does a muscle fibre do when the muscle is working?
104709.e: When the muscle fibre gets a signal from the nerve, it contracts and gets shorter. That is how the muscle pulls on the bone.

104710.q: What gives a muscle fibre the signal to contract?
104710.e: The brain sends electrical signals through nerves to the muscles. Only then do the muscle fibres contract.
104710.m: Nerves give the muscles the starting signal.

104711.q: Why is a muscle tired after long training?
a: The energy in the muscle fibres is running out
104711.e: Muscle fibres need a lot of energy. After long effort the supplies run low and waste products build up. Then the strength fades.
104711.m: Tired muscles have used up their energy supplies.

104712.q: Which muscle fibres have especially good endurance?
104712.e: Type I fibres have many mitochondria and lots of red muscle pigment. They tire slowly and are suited to endurance.
104712.m: Red muscle fibres have endurance; white ones are fast.

104713.q: What mainly happens to muscle fibres with regular strength training?
104713.e: Strength training mainly increases the cross-section of the fibres. This is called hypertrophy.
104713.m: Strength training makes muscle fibres thicker.

104714.q: Which substance directly supplies the muscle fibre with energy for contraction?
104714.e: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the cell’s direct energy carrier. Without ATP, actin and myosin cannot move.
104714.m: ATP is the muscle fibre’s fuel.

104715.q: What is the sheath of tough connective tissue around a whole muscle called?
104715.e: The muscle fascia wraps the muscle, holds the bundles of fibres together and lets neighbouring muscles glide past each other.
104715.m: A fascia wraps the whole muscle.

a: A sudden, painful tightening of a muscle
104716.e: In a muscle cramp, a muscle contracts involuntarily and stays painfully hard.
104716.m: A cramp is an unwanted, painful tightening of a muscle.

104717.q: Where do muscle cramps happen especially often?
104717.e: The calf muscles cramp most often, frequently at night or during sport.
104717.m: The calf is a common place for cramps.

104718.q: What usually helps straight away against a calf cramp?
104718.e: Gently stretching the cramped muscle usually makes the cramp go away after a short time.
104718.m: You relieve a cramp by stretching gently.

104719.q: Which way do you pull your toes to relieve a calf cramp?
a: Not at all, you let them hang
104719.e: If you pull your toes towards the shin, the calf muscles are stretched and the cramp eases.
104719.m: For a calf cramp, pull your toes towards your shin.

104720.q: What can make a muscle cramp during sport more likely?
a: Great tiredness and lots of sweating
104720.e: Overworked muscles and the loss of water and salts through sweating can trigger cramps.
104720.m: Tired muscles and fluid loss encourage cramps.

104721.q: How long does an ordinary muscle cramp usually last?
104721.e: An ordinary cramp is very painful but usually goes away after seconds to a few minutes.
104721.m: A normal cramp passes after a short time.

104722.q: When should you see a doctor about muscle cramps?
a: If they happen very often or for no reason
104722.e: Occasional cramps are usually harmless. But if they happen often, you should have the cause checked.
104722.m: Frequent cramps should be checked by a doctor.

104723.q: Which way of preventing cramps during sport makes sense?
a: Drinking enough and warming up well
Sprinting straight away without warming up
104723.e: Drinking enough, warming up and stretching help to prevent cramps.
104723.m: Drinking and warming up prevent cramps.

104724.e: With a strain, the muscle is stretched beyond its normal length. Tiny injuries occur, but there is no visible tear.
104724.m: A strain is an overstretching of the muscle.

104725.q: Which injury is more serious than a pulled muscle?
104725.e: With a torn muscle fibre, individual fibres really do tear. That is more serious than a strain and takes longer to heal.
104725.m: A torn muscle fibre is worse than a strain.

104726.q: What does the “I” in the first aid rule RICE stand for?
104726.e: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression (a pressure bandage) and Elevation. In German-speaking Switzerland the same rule is called PECH.
104726.m: The RICE rule means Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation.

104727.q: What should you do first after pulling a muscle?
104727.e: The strain must stop at once so that the injured muscle isn’t damaged even more.
104727.m: With a strain, stop the sport immediately.

104728.q: What does a pulled muscle typically feel like?
104728.e: A strain usually shows itself as a sudden, shooting, pulling pain that gets worse with movement.
104728.m: A strain hurts with a pulling, cramp-like pain.

104729.q: What increases the risk of a pulled muscle?
104729.e: Cold, unprepared muscles stretch less well and get injured more easily with sudden movements.

104730.q: With which movements do strains happen especially often?
a: Fast sprints and changes of direction
104730.e: Sudden, explosive movements such as sudden starts or stops put a lot of strain on the muscle.
104730.m: Sudden starts and stops can strain muscles.

104731.q: About how long does a mild pulled muscle take to heal?
a: A few days to a few weeks
104731.e: A mild strain usually heals in a few days to a few weeks. You should start using the muscle again slowly.
104731.m: A strain takes days to weeks to heal.

104732.q: What does the masseter (chewing muscle) do?
104732.e: The masseter pulls the lower jaw up and so closes the mouth when you bite.
104732.m: The masseter closes the jaw when you bite.

104733.q: Where can you feel the masseter when you clench your teeth hard?
a: At the side of the cheek in front of the ear
On the back of the head
104733.e: When you clench, the muscle bulges out at the side of the cheek and becomes hard.
104733.m: When you bite, you can feel the masseter on your cheek.

104734.q: Why should you chew your food thoroughly?
a: It is broken up and mixed with saliva
104734.e: The chewing muscles grind the food with the teeth. Well-chewed food mixes with saliva and is easier to swallow and digest.

104735.q: Which muscle at the temple is also one of the chewing muscles?
a: Neck muscle that turns the head
104735.e: The temporal muscle (musculus temporalis) also lifts the lower jaw. You can feel it at your temple when you chew.
104735.m: The temporal muscle helps with chewing too.

104736.q: What happens if you chew gum for a very long time?
104736.e: Chewing muscles also get tired when they work for a long time. Too much chewing can make them tense and sore.
104736.m: Chewing muscles can get tired too.

104737.q: What is the masseter known for?
a: It can produce a great deal of force for its size
It is the longest muscle in the body
104737.e: The masseter is short and thick and can build up a very strong bite.
104737.m: The small masseter is amazingly strong.

104738.q: What do you call pressing and grinding the teeth without noticing, often at night?
104738.e: When you grind your teeth (bruxism), the chewing muscles work hard. That can wear down teeth and make the muscles tense.
104738.m: Teeth grinding overworks the chewing muscles.

104739.q: Which type of muscle is the masseter?
104739.e: The masseter is striated and can be moved at will. That is why it is a skeletal muscle.
104739.m: You move the masseter on purpose; it is a skeletal muscle.

104740.q: What shape is the large chest muscle (pectoralis major)?
104740.e: The large chest muscle spreads like a fan across the chest and narrows towards the upper arm.
104740.m: The large chest muscle is shaped like a fan.

104741.q: Where is the large chest muscle attached?
a: To the back edge of the shoulder blade
104741.e: Its tendon runs from the chest under the deltoid to the humerus.
104741.m: The large chest muscle is attached to the upper arm.

104742.q: Which movement does the large chest muscle make?
a: It pulls the arm in towards the body
104742.e: The muscle pulls the arm in towards the trunk and turns it inwards, for example when you give someone a hug.
104742.m: The chest muscle pulls the arm towards the body.

104744.q: Which exercise especially trains the large chest muscle?
104744.e: In the bench press the barbell is pushed away from the chest. The chest muscle and triceps do most of the work.
104744.m: The bench press strengthens the large chest muscle.

104745.q: Where does part of the large chest muscle start?
104745.e: Among other places, the muscle starts at the breastbone, the collarbone and the rib cartilages.
104745.m: The large chest muscle starts at the breastbone, among other places.

104746.q: How can the large chest muscle help with breathing?
a: As a helper breathing muscle when the arms are propped up
104746.e: If you prop your arms up, the muscle can lift the rib cage and help you breathe in, for example after great effort.
104746.m: With your arms propped up, the chest muscle helps you breathe.

104747.q: Which muscle lies directly under the large chest muscle?
104747.e: Under the large chest muscle lies the smaller, triangular small chest muscle. It is attached to the shoulder blade.
104747.m: The small chest muscle lies under the large one.

104748.q: What happens to the arm when the large chest muscle contracts while the arm is stretched out to the side?
a: It is brought forwards towards the middle of the body
104748.e: The muscle brings the outstretched arm forwards to the middle, as when you clap in front of your chest.
104748.m: The chest muscle brings the arms together in front of the chest.

104749.q: Which two muscle groups mainly make up the core muscles?
104749.e: Tummy muscles at the front and sides and back muscles behind surround the trunk like a corset.
104749.m: Tummy and back muscles make up the core muscles.

104750.q: What is the main job of the core muscles?
104750.e: The core muscles keep the upper body upright and protect the spine from bad strain.
104750.m: The core muscles support the spine.

104751.e: The straight tummy muscle is divided into sections by tendons running across it. With little fat, you can see these sections.
104751.m: The straight tummy muscle forms the six-pack.

104752.q: Which exercise trains the core muscles well without you moving?
104752.e: In the plank you hold your body straight like a board. Tummy and back muscles work together.
104752.m: The plank strengthens the whole core.

104753.q: What is the muscle group called that straightens the back along the spine?
104753.e: The back extensors run on both sides of the spine from the pelvis to the head and straighten the trunk.
104753.m: The back extensors keep the back upright.

104754.q: Which tummy muscle lies deepest and works like a belt around the tummy?
104754.e: The transverse tummy muscle runs horizontally around the tummy. It tightens the tummy wall like a belt.
104754.m: The transverse tummy muscle wraps round the tummy like a belt.

104755.q: Between which areas does the straight tummy muscle run?
a: Between the rib cage and the pelvis
Between the shoulder and the elbow
Between the neck and the head
Between the knee and the foot
104755.e: The straight tummy muscle runs down the middle at the front from the lower rib cage to the pubic bone of the pelvis.
104755.m: The straight tummy muscle connects the rib cage and pelvis.

104756.q: What can weak core muscles lead to?
104756.e: Without strong core muscles, the spine lacks support. That can lead to poor posture and back pain.
104756.m: A strong core protects against back pain.

104757.q: Which muscles help when you sit up from lying down?
a: Straight tummy muscle and hip flexors
104757.e: The straight tummy muscle curls the upper body up, and the hip flexors pull it further up.
104757.m: When you sit up, tummy muscles and hip flexors work together.

104758.q: What are the facial expression muscles responsible for?
104758.e: Facial expression muscles change the face. That is how we can show joy, anger or amazement.
104758.m: Facial expression muscles shape the look on our face.

104759.q: Unlike most skeletal muscles, what are many facial expression muscles attached to?
104759.e: Facial expression muscles run from bone or connective tissue to the skin. That is why the skin of the face moves with them.
104759.m: Facial expression muscles pull on the skin of the face.

104760.q: Which nerve controls the facial expression muscles?
104760.e: The facial nerve is the seventh cranial nerve. If it is paralysed, one half of the face droops.
104760.m: The facial nerve controls facial expressions.

104761.e: The ring muscle of the eye (musculus orbicularis oculi) surrounds the eye and closes the lids when you blink.
104761.m: The ring muscle of the eye closes the lids.

104762.q: Which muscle shapes the lips when you whistle or pucker up for a kiss?
104762.e: The ring muscle of the mouth surrounds the lips like a ring. When it contracts, the lips are pursed.
104762.m: The ring muscle of the mouth purses the lips.

104763.q: Which muscle raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead into lines across it?
104763.e: When the forehead muscle contracts, the eyebrows go up and lines appear across the forehead, for example when you are amazed.
104763.m: The forehead muscle raises the eyebrows.

104764.q: Which muscle pulls the eyebrows together towards the middle when you frown?
104764.e: The corrugator (musculus corrugator supercilii) pulls the brows inwards and down. This creates vertical lines above the nose.
104764.m: The corrugator makes the lines between the eyebrows.

104765.q: Which facial muscle is also called the trumpeter’s muscle because it helps with blowing?
104765.e: The cheek muscle lies in the cheek and pushes air out of the mouth, for example when playing the trumpet.
104765.m: The cheek muscle helps with blowing.

104766.q: What do we mainly show with our facial expression muscles?
a: Feelings such as joy, anger or fear
104766.e: With our face muscles we laugh, look amazed or frown. That way others can see how we feel, even without words.
104766.m: We show our feelings with our facial expressions.

104866.q: Which type of root has a strong main root that grows straight down deep into the soil?
104866.e: In a taproot one thick main root dominates and grows straight down like a stake. The side roots are much weaker.
104866.m: A taproot grows straight down into the depths like a stake.

104867.q: Which broadleaved tree typically forms a strong taproot?
104867.e: Even as young plants, oaks push a long taproot deep into the soil. This anchors them very well.
104867.m: The oak is a typical tree with a taproot.

104868.q: Why is a tree with a taproot especially stable in a storm?
a: It is anchored deep in the ground
It loses all its leaves in the storm
104868.e: The taproot reaches far down and holds the tree like an anchor. That is why it is less often uprooted.
104868.m: A deep taproot holds a tree like an anchor.

104869.q: What does the main root of a taproot develop from?
a: From a bud on the trunk
104869.e: When a seed germinates, the first root comes out first. In many plants it grows straight on into the taproot.
104869.m: The taproot develops from the first root of the seed.

104870.q: What is the advantage of a taproot during a long drought?
a: It reaches water in deep layers of soil
It catches dew from the air
It does photosynthesis in the soil
It stores water in the leaves
104870.e: When the upper layers of soil dry out, there is often still water deeper down. Taproots can reach this water.
104870.m: Taproots get water even from great depths.

104871.q: Which lawn plant has a long taproot that is hard to pull out?
104871.e: The dandelion forms a long, fleshy taproot. If a piece stays in the ground, it often grows again.
104871.m: The dandelion holds firmly in the ground with its long taproot.

104872.q: Which group of plants usually forms one continuous main root with side roots?
104872.e: In dicots the first root usually remains as the main root. Grasses, on the other hand, form many fibrous roots of equal thickness.
104872.m: Dicots usually have a main root with side roots.

104873.q: What are plants called whose roots reach especially far down?
104873.e: Plants with a taproot are deep-rooted. Their roots reach deep layers of soil.
104873.m: Deep-rooted plants send their roots far down.

104874.q: Roughly what shape is the root system of a heart-rooted tree?
a: Like a dome or a heart
104874.e: In a heart root system several strong roots grow slanting downwards and outwards. In outline this gives a heart-shaped to dome-shaped form.
104874.m: A heart root system has the outline of a heart.

104875.q: Which forest tree has a typical heart root system?
104875.e: The common beech forms a strong heart root system. Its roots grow at a slant in all directions to a medium depth.
104875.m: The common beech has heart roots.

104876.q: A heart root is a mix of which two root types?
104876.e: Heart roots reach deeper than shallow roots, but not as deep as taproots. So they lie between these two types.
104876.m: The heart root lies between taproot and shallow root.

104877.q: Which of these conifers has heart roots?
104877.e: The larch forms a heart root system with several strong roots growing downwards at a slant. The spruce has shallow roots; Scots pine and silver fir form taproots.
104877.m: The larch is a conifer with heart roots.

104878.q: Which of these trees has heart roots?
104878.e: Lime trees form a heart root system with several main roots growing downwards at a slant. Spruces have shallow roots; oaks and silver firs form taproots.
104878.m: The lime also has heart roots.

104879.q: Why are heart-rooted trees usually quite storm-proof?
a: Their roots anchor them on all sides
They only grow sheltered from the wind
104879.e: The roots of a heart-rooted tree grip into the soil at a slant in all directions. This holds the tree evenly.
104879.m: Heart-rooted trees are anchored in the soil on all sides.

104880.q: For which plants do people mainly talk about heart-rooted, taprooted and shallow-rooted types?
104880.e: The division into heart-rooted, taprooted and shallow-rooted is mainly used for trees and shrubs. It is important in forestry, for example.
104880.m: The division by root shape is mainly used for trees.

104881.q: What does a typical heart root lack compared with a taproot?
104881.e: In a heart root several roots of similar strength share the work. There is no single main root that dominates everything.
104881.m: A heart root has several equally strong main roots instead of just one.

104882.q: Which common conifer has shallow roots and is often blown over in storms?
104882.e: The spruce spreads its roots out like a plate just below the surface. That is why it can easily topple in strong wind.
104882.m: The spruce has shallow roots and is therefore at risk in storms.
