106478.m: Fir wood contains hardly any resin.

106479.q: Which scented plant with whorled leaves often grows on the floor of beech and fir and beech forests?
106479.e: Sweet woodruff forms small carpets in shady mixed broadleaved forests. Its leaves stand in a star around the stem and smell of hay when dried.
106479.m: Sweet woodruff grows in the shade of beeches and firs.

106480.q: What is the wood of slow-growing mountain spruces especially sought after for?
a: For floors in indoor swimming pools
For garden fences in the sea
106480.e: Spruces from high, cold places have very even, narrow growth rings. This tonewood vibrates well and is valued in instrument making, for example from the Risoud forest in the Jura.
106480.m: Mountain spruces provide valuable tonewood for instruments.

106481.q: Why are spruces increasingly at risk in low, warm areas of the Swiss Plateau?
a: They suffer from heat and drought
The ground there is too cold
106481.e: The spruce is really a tree of cool mountain forests. In warm lowlands, planted spruces get stressed in droughts and become vulnerable to pests.
106481.m: In warm lowlands the spruce is at a disadvantage with climate change.

106482.q: Which bird with crossed beak tips gets the seeds out of spruce cones?
106482.e: With its crossed beak it prises the cone scales apart. It even breeds in winter if there are enough cones.
106482.m: The common crossbill specialises in spruce seeds.

106483.q: Which dwarf shrub shapes the undergrowth of many acidic subalpine spruce forests?
106483.e: The bilberry loves acidic, humus-rich soils and light shade. That is why it often forms dense carpets in mountain spruce forests.
106483.m: Bilberries often grow on the ground in mountain spruce forests.

106484.q: What does fallen spruce needle litter do to the soil over time?
a: It makes the soil more acidic
It has no effect at all
106484.e: Spruce needles break down only slowly and form an acidic layer of humus. Many plants and soil animals do not like such soils.
106484.m: Spruce needles make the forest soil acidic.

106485.q: Roughly how tall can spruces grow?
106485.e: Spruces usually reach 30 to 50 metres, and single trees a little more. This makes them some of the tallest trees in Europe.
106485.m: Spruces can grow about 50 metres tall.

106486.q: What do you call a forest where almost only spruces of the same age have been planted over a large area?
106486.e: In the past, pure spruce stands were often planted on the Swiss Plateau because the spruce grows fast. But such monocultures are vulnerable to storms, drought and pests.
106486.m: Spruce monocultures grow fast but are vulnerable.

106487.q: Why is it rather dark all year round on the floor of a dense spruce forest?
a: Spruces keep their needles even in winter
Spruces lose all their needles in autumn
Spruce forests always stand in gorges
106487.e: As evergreen trees, spruces keep their dense canopy all year. Unlike in a broadleaved forest, there is no bright period in spring.
106487.m: A dense spruce forest is shady all year round.

106488.q: In which areas of Switzerland are larch and stone pine forests especially widespread?
106488.e: Larch and stone pine forests love the dry climate of the inner Alpine valleys with cold winters and lots of sun. The spruce does less well there.
106488.m: In the Engadine and Valais larches and stone pines shape the mountain forests.

106489.q: Which well-known forest at Riederalp is an old larch and stone pine forest?
106489.e: The Aletsch Forest lies above the Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.
106489.m: The Aletsch Forest is a famous stone pine and larch forest in Valais.

106490.q: Why does a lot of grass and herbs often grow under larches, so that cattle can graze there?
a: The open larch crown lets a lot of light through
Larches fertilise the soil with sugar
106490.e: Larches have a loose crown with fine needles. The light reaches the ground, which is why grazed larch meadows form in the mountains.
106490.m: Larch forests are open and let grass grow.

106491.q: Which tree of the larch and stone pine forest is usually the first to settle open areas such as avalanche tracks or land in front of glaciers?
106491.e: The larch needs a lot of light and grows fast when young. As a pioneer tree it conquers open ground, while the stone pine follows later.
106491.m: The larch is a typical pioneer tree of the Alps.

106492.q: How fast does the Swiss stone pine grow?
a: Only in its first two years
106492.e: High up, the growing season is short, and the stone pine adds only a little wood each year. That is why its wood has very narrow growth rings.
106492.m: The Swiss stone pine grows very slowly.

106493.q: Why is the larch well protected from drying out in winter?
a: Without needles it loses hardly any water
It stores water in its cones
It drinks snow through its bark
106493.e: When the ground is frozen, trees cannot take up more water. Evergreen trees still lose water through their needles, but the bare larch hardly does.
106493.m: The bare larch is protected from frost drought.

106494.q: Which moth regularly eats whole larch forests brown in the Engadine?
106494.e: The caterpillars of this moth multiply in huge numbers about every eight to ten years and eat the needles. The larches usually grow new needles afterwards.
106494.m: The larch bud moth turns larch forests brown in some years.

106495.q: Roughly how tall can larches grow?
106495.e: Larches usually grow 30 to 40 metres tall. High up at the forest line, though, they often stay much smaller because of the harsh climate.
106495.m: Larches can grow about 40 metres tall.

106496.q: What is typical of a floodplain forest?
a: It is regularly flooded by a river
106496.e: Floodplain forests lie along rivers and streams whose water level changes a lot. In floods they are under water, and afterwards they dry out again.
106496.m: Floodplain forests live with regular flooding.

106499.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland’s floodplains has disappeared over time?
106499.e: Rivers were straightened and walled in, and floodplains were drained and built on. Only a small remnant of the original floodplains is left.
106499.m: Most of Switzerland’s floodplains have disappeared.

106500.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland’s land area do floodplains still cover today?
106500.e: Floodplains have shrunk to a very small part of the country’s area. Even so, they are home to a huge variety of living things.
106500.m: Floodplains cover only a tiny part of Switzerland.

106501.q: Why are floodplains seen as habitats especially rich in species?
a: There is never any water there
A lot of fertiliser is used there
Only a few plants grow there
106501.e: Floods drop gravel and sand, tear open banks and form new ponds. This creates an ever-changing patchwork in which about half of all Swiss plant species are found.
106501.m: The movement of the water makes floodplains so rich in species.

106503.q: What does the Confederation protect with the Federal Inventory of Floodplains of National Importance?
a: The most valuable floodplains in Switzerland
106503.e: Since 1992, especially valuable floodplains have been protected by the Confederation. The inventory now includes more than 300 areas.
106503.m: The Confederation protects the most important floodplains in Switzerland.

106504.q: Roughly what share of Swiss forest has a protective function?
106504.e: According to federal surveys, about half of the Swiss forest area counts as protection forest. The share is especially large in the Alpine cantons.
106504.m: About half of Swiss forest is protection forest.

106505.q: How does a forest protect against avalanches?
a: The trees hold the snow in place
The trees blow the snow away
106505.e: The many tree trunks hold the snow in place on the slope. So it cannot slide down as a big avalanche.
106505.m: Trees hold the snow in place on the slope.

106506.q: How does a forest protect against falling rocks?
a: The trunks slow down and stop falling rocks
106506.e: A falling rock hits trunks and loses energy. In this way a dense, healthy forest with many trunks holds back a lot of rocks.
106506.m: Tree trunks act as a brake against falling rocks.

106507.q: Why is looking after protection forest often cheaper than technical protective structures?
a: A well-kept forest protects for a long time at much lower cost
106507.e: Avalanche barriers and rockfall nets are expensive to build and maintain. A protection forest that is looked after does its job year after year for a fraction of that.
106507.m: A well-kept protection forest is cheap protection.

106508.q: What is a ‘Bannwald’, like the one Andermatt already had in the Middle Ages?
a: A forest where felling was banned so it would protect against avalanches
A forest where only the king was allowed to hunt
A forest that was burnt to gain grazing land
A forest where criminals were abandoned
106508.e: With a written ban, the valley people forbade the use of the forest above the village. So it stayed dense and protected Andermatt from avalanches. The protected forest of Andermatt is still well known today.
106508.m: A Bannwald could not be cut down because it protected against avalanches.

106509.q: Which animals threaten the young trees in protection forest when their numbers are too high?
a: Red deer, roe deer and chamois
106509.e: These plant-eaters eat the buds and shoots of young trees. Without young trees, the protection forest cannot keep doing its job in the long run.
106509.m: Too many deer can stop the protection forest from renewing itself.

106510.q: How does a forest help against landslides and erosion on steep slopes?
a: The roots hold the soil together
The crowns make the soil heavier
The bark draws water out of the rock
106510.e: A dense network of roots anchors the soil like a net. The forest floor also stores a lot of rainwater and releases it slowly.
106510.m: Roots hold the soil in place on the slope.

106511.q: What is built above the forest so that the snow cover there does not slide off as an avalanche?
106511.e: Snow supporting structures made of steel or wood hold the snow cover in place on steep slopes. Up there they do the job that the forest does further down.
106511.m: Snow supporting structures replace the forest where none grows.

106512.q: Why does a protection forest need to be looked after regularly?
a: So that young trees always grow up
So that it stays as dark as possible
So that it does not grow roots
So that no animals live there
106512.e: If a forest has only trees of the same age, many can collapse at the same time. That is why foresters create gaps where young trees can grow.
106512.m: A protection forest needs trees of every age.

106513.q: What is typical of a selection forest?
a: Trees of all ages grow side by side
All the trees are the same age
There is only a single layer of trees
106513.e: In a selection forest, small, medium and large trees grow closely mixed on the same area. This creates a layered structure from the ground up to the crowns.
106513.m: In a selection forest young and old trees stand side by side.

106514.q: How is a selection forest used?
a: The whole forest is felled at once
106514.e: The forester keeps removing single trees that are mature or in the way. This keeps the forest closed all the time and renewing itself constantly.
106514.m: In a selection forest only single trees are removed.

106515.q: Which tree species make up the classic Swiss selection forests?
a: Stone pine, larch and dwarf mountain pine
106515.e: These three tree species can survive as young trees in the shade of the big ones. This is what makes it possible for all ages to grow side by side.
106515.m: Fir, spruce and beech make up the typical selection forest.

106516.q: Which Swiss region is regarded as classic selection forest country?
106516.e: The farmers’ forests in the Emmental have been managed by selection for generations. Some of the most impressive selection forests in Europe stand there.
106516.m: The Emmental is known for its selection forests.

106517.q: What does a forester in a selection forest measure regularly to know how much wood can be harvested?
106517.e: The Neuchâtel forester Henri Biolley measured the stock of timber regularly. So he harvested only as much as grew back.
106517.m: In a selection forest only as much wood is harvested as grows back.

106518.q: Which way of harvesting wood is basically banned in Swiss forests?
106518.e: The federal Forest Act bans clear-cutting, where large areas are felled all at once. The forest is meant to stay natural and last.

106519.q: Why is a selection forest good as a protection forest?
a: It is always closed and never has big gaps
It consists only of broadleaved trees
It only grows in the lowlands
106519.e: Because only single trees are ever missing, the ground stays covered by forest all the time. So the forest can do its protective job without a break.
106519.m: A selection forest protects all the time because it never becomes bare.

106520.q: What must young trees in a selection forest above all be able to cope with?
106520.e: Only a little light gets through the canopy of the big trees. Young trees there have to wait a long time until a gap opens.
106520.m: Young trees in a selection forest grow up in the shade.

106618.q: Where does the right atrium pass its blood on to?
106618.e: The right atrium contracts and pushes the blood through a valve into the right ventricle below it.
106618.m: Each atrium passes its blood to the ventricle on the same side.

106619.q: What is the technical term for one of the two upper chambers of the heart?
106619.e: In technical language, an upper chamber of the heart is called an atrium, the Latin word for entrance hall. Doctors speak of the right and left atrium.
106619.m: An upper chamber of the heart is called an atrium.

106620.q: Why do the atria have thinner muscle walls than the ventricles?
a: They only push the blood into the nearby ventricle.
They contain no blood at all.
106620.e: The atria only have to move the blood a short distance into the ventricles. This needs little force and so little muscle.
106620.m: The atria need little force and so have thin walls.

106621.q: What is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, in which the atria twitch irregularly, called?
106621.e: In atrial fibrillation, the atria no longer contract in an orderly way. It is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, especially in older people.
106621.m: Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder.

106622.q: Why does only a little blood flow through the lungs of an unborn baby?
a: Because it does not breathe yet and gets oxygen through the umbilical cord
Because it has no lungs yet
Because its heart does not beat yet
106622.e: Before birth, the baby gets oxygen through the umbilical cord. That is why most of the blood bypasses the lungs, partly through an opening between the atria.
106622.m: Before birth, most of the blood bypasses the lungs.

106624.q: Roughly how much blood does one ventricle of an adult pump out per heartbeat at rest?
106624.e: This stroke volume is around 70 millilitres at rest, which is about as much as five tablespoons. During sport it can rise a lot.
106624.m: Each ventricle pumps about 70 millilitres of blood per heartbeat.

106625.q: What is the sac of connective tissue that surrounds the whole heart called?
106625.e: The pericardium surrounds the heart like a cover. A thin layer of fluid inside it lets the heart glide smoothly as it beats.
106625.m: The pericardium protects the heart and lets it beat smoothly.

106626.q: How many valves does the human heart have?
106626.e: There are two valves between the atria and the ventricles and two at the exits of the ventricles. Together that makes four.

106627.q: What do you mainly hear when listening to the heart with a stethoscope?
a: The lungs rushing inside the heart
106627.e: The typical heart sounds are made when the heart valves close. In this way doctors can hear whether the valves are working properly.
106627.m: Heart sounds are made when the heart valves close.

106628.q: In which direction do the valves between atrium and ventricle let the blood flow?
a: From the atrium into the ventricle
From the ventricle into the atrium
Not at all, they are always shut
106628.e: The atria collect the blood and pass it on to the ventricles. The valves between them only let it through in this direction.
106628.m: Blood flows from the atrium into the ventricle.

106630.q: What makes the heart valves open and close?
a: Their own muscles in the valves
106630.e: Heart valves move without any force of their own. When blood pushes from one side they open, and when it pushes back they shut like a door in the wind.
106630.m: Blood pressure opens and closes the heart valves.

106631.q: What stops the flap valves from flipping back into the atria when the ventricles contract?
106631.e: Fine tendon cords connect the flaps to small muscles in the wall of the ventricle. They hold the flaps in place like the lines of a parachute.
106631.m: Tendon cords hold the flap valves in position.

106633.q: What is the curved section of the aorta just above the heart called?
106633.e: The aorta first rises upwards and then bends backwards and downwards in an arch. The arteries for the head and arms branch off from the aortic arch.
106633.m: The aortic arch lies just above the heart.

106634.q: Which vessels are the first to branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself?
106634.e: The coronary arteries branch off just after the aortic valve. They lie around the heart like a crown and supply it with oxygen.
106634.m: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with blood.

106635.q: What kind of blood flows in the aorta?
106635.e: The blood in the aorta comes straight from the heart after it has picked up fresh oxygen in the lungs. That is why it is rich in oxygen.
106635.m: Oxygen-rich blood flows in the aorta.

106636.q: Why is the aorta the largest artery in the body?
a: All the blood from the left ventricle flows through it
It brings blood back to the heart
It carries air to the lungs
106636.e: The left ventricle pumps the oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. All the arteries of the body’s circulation branch off from it.
106636.m: The aorta is the largest artery in the body.

106637.q: How many venae cavae lead into the heart?
106637.e: There is a superior (upper) and an inferior (lower) vena cava. Both bring blood from the body to the heart.
106637.m: An upper and a lower vena cava lead to the heart.

106638.q: Which chamber of the heart do the venae cavae lead into?
106638.e: Both venae cavae end in the right atrium. That is where the blood’s journey to the lungs begins.
106638.m: The venae cavae lead into the right atrium.

106639.q: From which parts of the body does the superior vena cava collect blood?
a: From the head, neck and arms
106639.e: The superior vena cava brings the blood back from the upper half of the body. This includes the head, neck and arms.
106639.m: The superior vena cava brings blood back from the head and arms.

106640.q: From which areas of the body does the blood in the inferior vena cava come?
106640.e: The inferior vena cava collects the blood from the lower body. It runs up next to the spine to the heart.
106640.m: The inferior vena cava brings blood back from the legs and abdomen.

106641.q: What kind of blood do the venae cavae carry?
106641.e: The blood has given up its oxygen to the organs before it reaches the venae cavae. That is why it is low in oxygen and darker.
106641.m: Used, oxygen-poor blood flows in the venae cavae.

106642.q: Which is the largest vein in the human body?
106642.e: The inferior vena cava has the largest diameter of all veins. It carries the blood of the whole lower half of the body.
106642.m: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein in the body.

106643.q: Where do the venae cavae take the blood?
106643.e: The superior and inferior venae cavae collect the blood from the body and take it back to the heart.
106643.m: The venae cavae take the blood back to the heart.

106644.q: What is the pulmonary circulation also called?
106644.e: The pulmonary circulation only goes from the heart to the lungs and back. Because the route is short, it is called the small circulation.
106644.m: The pulmonary circulation is the small circulation.

106645.q: In which chamber of the heart does the pulmonary circulation begin?
106645.e: The right ventricle pumps the oxygen-poor blood towards the lungs. That is where the pulmonary circulation begins.
106645.m: The pulmonary circulation begins in the right ventricle.

106646.q: Where does the pulmonary circulation end?
106646.e: The fresh blood flows from the lungs back to the heart and reaches the left atrium there. This closes the small circulation.
106646.m: The pulmonary circulation ends in the left atrium.

106647.q: How does blood pressure in the pulmonary circulation compare with the body’s circulation?
106647.e: The lungs are close to the heart, and the delicate air sacs cannot cope with high pressure. That is why the pressure in the pulmonary circulation is much lower.
106647.m: Blood pressure is low in the pulmonary circulation.

106648.q: Which blood vessels bring the blood from the lungs back to the heart?
106648.e: After the exchange of gases, the pulmonary veins collect the fresh blood. They take it back to the heart.
106648.m: The pulmonary veins bring fresh blood from the lungs to the heart.

106649.q: What is the body’s circulation (systemic circulation) also called?
106649.e: The body’s circulation supplies the whole body from head to toe. Because it reaches so far, it is called the large circulation.
106649.m: The body’s circulation is the large circulation.

106650.q: In which chamber of the heart does the body’s circulation begin?
106650.e: The left ventricle pumps the oxygen-rich blood into the body. From there it spreads to all the organs.
106650.m: The body’s circulation begins in the left ventricle.

106651.q: What happens to the ventricles during systole?
a: They contract and pump blood out.
106651.e: During systole, the muscles of the ventricles contract. This pushes the blood into the large arteries.
106651.m: In systole, the ventricles pump the blood out.

106652.q: Where do the ventricles pump the blood during systole?
a: Into the large arteries such as the aorta
106652.e: The ventricles contract and push the blood into the large arteries. Valves stop it from flowing back into the atria.
106652.m: In systole, the blood flows into the arteries.

106653.q: What does the Greek word “systole” literally mean?
106653.e: Systole comes from Greek and means contraction. That is exactly what the heart muscle does in this phase.

106654.q: What happens to the ventricles during diastole?
a: They relax and fill with blood.
They push blood into the aorta.
106654.e: Diastole is the phase of relaxing and filling. The muscles of the ventricles relax, and blood flows in from the atria.
106654.m: In diastole, the ventricles relax and fill.

106655.q: Where does the blood flow into the ventricles from while they relax in diastole?
106655.e: During diastole, the flap valves open. So blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.
106655.m: In diastole, blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.

106656.q: What is the phase called in which the ventricles contract and push blood out?
106656.e: In systole, the ventricles contract and pump blood into the arteries. In diastole, they relax and fill again.
106656.m: Systole means pumping, diastole means relaxing and filling.

106657.q: Which reading when measuring blood pressure belongs to diastole?
106657.e: In 120 over 80, the 80 is the diastolic reading. It shows the pressure in the arteries while the heart relaxes.
106657.m: The lower blood pressure reading is the diastolic one.

106658.q: Which phase lasts longer in a calm heartbeat?
a: Neither, there is only one phase
106658.e: At rest, the relaxing and filling phase takes up about two thirds of a heartbeat. This gives the ventricles enough time to fill.
106658.m: At rest, diastole lasts longer than systole.

106659.q: What happens during a heart attack?
a: A blood vessel of the heart gets blocked and part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen
The heart suddenly becomes twice as big
106659.e: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with blood. If one of them closes, the affected part of the heart muscle dies without quick help.
106659.m: In a heart attack, part of the heart muscle lacks oxygen.

106660.q: What is a stent, which is often used after a heart attack?
a: A small mesh tube that holds a vessel open
106660.e: A stent is pushed into the narrowed vessel with a catheter and widened there. It supports the vessel wall so that the blood can flow again.
106660.m: A stent holds a narrowed vessel open.

106661.q: What is a defibrillator used for?
a: To stop a dangerous heart rhythm with an electric shock
To blow oxygen into the lungs
106661.e: A defibrillator gives a strong electric shock. This can stop a chaotic heart rhythm so that the heart can beat normally again.
106661.m: A defibrillator uses electricity to stop a life-threatening heart rhythm.

106662.q: What does the abbreviation AED stand for?
106662.e: An AED is a device for ordinary people that analyses the heart rhythm by itself. In Switzerland, devices like this hang in many railway stations, schools and sports grounds.
106662.m: An AED is an automatic defibrillator for everyone.

106663.q: Which heart rhythm disorder can be stopped with a defibrillator?
106663.e: In ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles twitch chaotically and no longer pump blood. An electric shock can end this chaos.
106663.m: Ventricular fibrillation is life-threatening and is treated with a defibrillator.

106664.q: Can a person with no medical training use an AED?
a: Yes, the device gives spoken instructions.
106664.e: An AED explains every step with spoken instructions. It only gives a shock if it detects a suitable rhythm.
106664.m: Anyone may and should use an AED in an emergency.

106665.q: Where do you stick the pads of an AED?
a: On the soles of the feet
On the back over the clothes
106665.e: The sticky pads go on the bare skin of the upper body. The pads have a picture showing exactly where they belong.
106665.m: You stick the pads of an AED on the bare chest.

106666.q: What must you remember while the AED gives a shock?
a: You must hold the person tight.
You must pour water over the chest.
106666.e: Otherwise the electric shock could also pass to the helpers. That is why the device tells everyone to stand clear.
106666.m: Nobody touches the person during the shock.

106667.q: How fast should you press during chest compressions?
106667.e: The guidelines recommend a rate of 100 to 120 compressions a minute. That is about the beat of a fast pop song.
106667.m: In chest compressions you press 100 to 120 times a minute.

106668.q: How deep should you press down an adult’s chest during chest compressions?
a: Not at all, just touch it
106668.e: For effective chest compressions, the chest is pressed down about 5 to 6 centimetres. Only then is enough blood pushed around the body.
106668.m: In adults you press the chest down about five to six centimetres.

106669.q: What is a defibrillator placed under the skin called?
106669.e: An implantable defibrillator, ICD for short, constantly monitors the heart rhythm. If ventricular fibrillation happens, it gives a shock by itself.
106669.m: An implantable defibrillator watches over the heart around the clock.

a: In the wall of the right atrium
106670.e: The sinus node is a small group of special heart muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium. Every normal heartbeat starts there.
106670.m: The sinus node is in the right atrium.

106671.q: What job does the sinus node have in the heart?
a: It sets the rhythm of the heartbeat
106671.e: The sinus node sends out electrical impulses regularly. Each impulse triggers a heartbeat, which is why it is called the heart’s pacemaker.
106671.m: The sinus node is the heart’s pacemaker.

106672.q: What is put in when the heart’s natural pacemaker no longer works properly?
106672.e: A pacemaker is a small device under the skin. It gives electrical impulses when the heart beats too slowly.
106672.m: A pacemaker replaces a weak natural pacemaker.

106673.q: How does the resting pulse often change in well-trained endurance athletes?
a: It is lower than in untrained people.
It goes up and down a lot for no reason.
106673.e: A trained heart pumps more blood with each beat. That is why it needs fewer beats at rest, often under 60 a minute.
106673.m: Training can lower the resting pulse.

106674.q: Which signs of a heart attack appear more often in women than in men?
a: Nausea, shortness of breath and back pain
106674.e: In women, the typical chest pain is missing more often. Instead, nausea, shortness of breath or pain in the back or upper abdomen appear more often.
106674.m: A heart attack can also happen without chest pain.

106675.q: What can a biological replacement heart valve be made from?
106675.e: Biological heart valves are often made from tissue from pigs or cattle. There are also mechanical valves made of metal and plastic.
106675.m: Replacement heart valves are made of animal tissue or metal.

106676.q: What is the section of the aorta below the diaphragm called?
106676.e: The aorta passes through an opening in the diaphragm into the abdomen. There it is called the abdominal aorta and sends branches to the intestines and kidneys.
106676.m: Below the diaphragm, the aorta is called the abdominal aorta.

106677.q: Which part of the heart contracts first with every heartbeat?
106677.e: The electrical signal starts at the top of the heart. That is why the atria contract first and top up the filling of the ventricles, and only then do the ventricles follow.
106677.m: With every heartbeat, the atria contract first.

106678.q: How many atria does the human heart have?
106678.e: The heart has a right and a left atrium. Below each one lies a ventricle.
106678.m: The heart has two atria and two ventricles.

106679.q: What do the atria do while the ventricles contract?
a: They fill with blood from the veins.
They pump blood into the aorta.
106679.e: While the ventricles pump out blood, the atria are relaxed. During this time, new blood is already flowing into them from the veins.
106679.m: The atria fill up while the ventricles pump.

106680.q: A heart pumps 70 ml of blood per beat and beats 70 times a minute. Roughly how much blood does it pump per minute?
106680.e: 70 times 70 ml makes 4900 ml, so almost 5 litres. That is about all the blood of an adult going once round the body every minute.
106680.m: At rest the heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute.

106681.q: What is a congenital heart defect?
a: A fault in the heart that is already there at birth
A heart attack in old age
A pulse that is too fast after sport
A cold that affects the heart
106681.e: Congenital heart defects develop while the heart is growing in the womb. One example is a hole in the wall between the ventricles. Many can be treated well today.
106681.m: A congenital heart defect is already there at birth.

106682.q: What is the wall of the ventricles mainly made of?
106682.e: The wall of the heart is mainly made of heart muscle. When it contracts, the blood is pushed out of the ventricles.
106682.m: The ventricles are surrounded by strong muscles.

106683.q: Why is the inside of the ventricles completely smooth?
a: So that the blood flows freely and does not clot
So that the heart is lighter
So that you can hear the heart beating
106683.e: A thin, smooth lining covers the chambers and valves of the heart. Blood clots could form more easily on rough spots.
106683.m: The smooth inner lining of the heart helps the blood flow well.

106684.q: What share of the blood in a healthy left ventricle is pumped out with each heartbeat?
106684.e: A healthy left ventricle pumps out about 55 to 70 per cent of its contents with each beat. This share is called the ejection fraction.
106684.m: A healthy ventricle pumps out more than half its blood with each beat.

106685.q: Where does the blood flow when the valve at the exit of the left ventricle opens?
106685.e: The aortic valve sits at the exit of the left ventricle. When it opens, oxygen-rich blood flows into the aorta and from there to the whole body.
106685.m: From the left ventricle, the blood flows into the aorta.

106686.q: What does the heart have to do if a heart valve is narrowed and no longer opens wide?
106686.e: Blood can only be pushed through a narrow opening with more force. In the long run this overloads the heart muscle, which is why severe narrowing is treated.
106686.m: With a narrowed valve, the heart has to work harder.

106687.q: What happens if a heart valve leaks?
a: Some of the blood flows back
106687.e: A leaky valve does not close completely. Some of the blood flows back, and the heart has to pump it again.
106687.m: With a leaky valve, blood flows back.

106688.q: Which large arteries that supply the head branch off from the aortic arch?
106688.e: Large branches go upwards from the aortic arch. From them come the carotid arteries for the head and brain and the arteries for the arms.
106688.m: The carotid arteries get their blood from the aortic arch.

106689.q: Roughly where does the aorta split into the two pelvic arteries?
a: At about the level of the belly button
106689.e: The aorta runs downwards in front of the spine. At about the level of the belly button, it forks into a left and a right pelvic artery.
106689.m: The aorta forks at about the level of the belly button.

106690.q: How does the blood pressure in the venae cavae near the heart compare with the aorta?
106690.e: On its long journey through arteries and capillaries, the blood loses almost all its pressure. That is why the pressure in the venae cavae near the heart is very low.
106690.m: Blood pressure in the venae cavae is very low.

106691.q: What is the large vessel called that comes out of the right ventricle and splits into a left and a right pulmonary artery?
106691.e: The pulmonary trunk comes out of the right ventricle. Shortly afterwards it splits into one artery for each lung.
106691.m: The pulmonary trunk splits into a left and a right pulmonary artery.

106692.q: Which Arab doctor was the first to describe the pulmonary circulation, in the 13th century?
106692.e: Ibn al-Nafis lived in Damascus and Cairo. He realised that blood travels from the right half of the heart through the lungs to the left half.
106692.m: Ibn al-Nafis described the pulmonary circulation in the 13th century.

106693.q: How many pulmonary veins normally lead into the human heart?
106693.e: Usually two pulmonary veins come from each lung. So together there are normally four.
106693.m: Normally four pulmonary veins lead to the heart.

106694.q: Why do we talk about the blood’s “circulation”?
a: The blood keeps flowing back to the heart
The blood flows in a circle around the tummy
106694.e: The heart pumps the blood through the arteries into the body. Through the veins it flows back to the heart, and everything starts again.
106694.m: The blood flows in a circle away from the heart and back again.

106695.q: What are the finest blood vessels, where oxygen is passed to the cells, called?
106695.e: Capillaries are thinner than a hair. Oxygen and nutrients reach the cells through their thin walls.
106695.m: In the capillaries, the blood passes oxygen to the cells.

106696.q: What share of all the blood is in the veins at rest?
106696.e: Veins are wide and stretchy and work like a blood store. Around two thirds of the blood is in them.
106696.m: The veins hold most of the blood.

106697.q: Which pair of organs receives about a fifth of the blood pumped out by the heart at rest?
106697.e: The kidneys constantly filter the blood and so have a very large blood supply. They get around 20 per cent of the heart’s output, even though they are small.
106697.m: The kidneys have an especially large blood supply.

106698.q: What happens to the small arteries in the skin in the cold?
106698.e: Narrowed skin vessels let less warm blood reach the surface of the body. So the body loses less heat, and the skin turns pale.
106698.m: In the cold, the blood vessels in the skin narrow.

106699.q: What is the phase after systole called, in which the heart relaxes and fills with blood?
106699.e: The heart switches between systole and diastole. In systole it pumps, in diastole it relaxes and fills again.

106700.q: What is the phase of systole called in which blood flows out of the ventricles?
106700.e: As soon as the pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the artery, the valve opens. Now the blood is pushed out.
106700.m: In the ejection phase, blood flows out of the ventricles.

106701.q: Which heart sound can be heard at the start of systole?
106701.e: At the start of systole, the flap valves close and the heart muscle tenses. This makes the first heart sound.
106701.m: The first heart sound marks the start of systole.

106702.e: In an extrasystole, the heart beats outside its normal rhythm. Single extrasystoles are common and usually harmless.
106702.m: An extrasystole is a heartbeat outside the normal rhythm.

106703.q: When is the pressure in the aorta highest?
106703.e: When the left ventricle pumps out blood, the pressure in the aorta rises to its highest value. Then it falls again until the next heartbeat.
106703.m: The pressure in the aorta is highest during systole.

106704.q: What do the ventricles do straight after diastole?
a: They stand still for a minute
106704.e: The filling phase is followed by systole. The ventricles contract and pump the blood into the body and the lungs.
106704.m: Diastole is always followed by systole.

106705.q: What does the Greek word “diastole” literally mean?
106705.e: Diastole comes from Greek and means expansion. In this phase the ventricles widen and take in blood.

106706.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland if you suspect a heart attack?
106706.e: 144 is the number for the ambulance. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 145 Tox Info Suisse for poisoning.
106706.m: If you suspect a heart attack, call 144 straight away.

106707.q: Which examination uses contrast dye to show narrowed coronary arteries?
106707.e: A thin tube is pushed along an artery up to the heart. With contrast dye and X-rays, doctors can see exactly where a vessel is narrowed.
106707.m: Cardiac catheterisation finds narrowed coronary arteries.

106708.q: What is the operation called in which a blocked coronary artery is bypassed with a piece of vessel?
106708.e: In a bypass, a piece of vein or artery is sewn on as a detour. So the blood flows past the blocked spot.
106708.m: A bypass is a detour around a blocked heart vessel.

106709.q: Which metabolic illness with permanently raised blood sugar increases the risk of a heart attack?
106709.e: Permanently high blood sugar damages the walls of the blood vessels. That is why people with diabetes have a higher risk of heart attacks.
106709.m: Diabetes damages the vessels and increases the risk of a heart attack.

106710.q: What do you count when you take a pulse?
a: How often the heart beats per minute
How often you breathe per minute
106710.e: With every heartbeat you feel a push in the arteries. If you count these pushes for one minute, you know the heart rate.
106710.m: The pulse shows how often the heart beats per minute.

106711.q: What happens to the pulse with a fever or great excitement?
a: It always stays exactly the same
106711.e: With a fever, excitement or exertion, the sinus node makes the heart beat faster. This gives the body more blood and oxygen.
106711.m: Fever and excitement make the pulse faster.

106712.q: How does the heartbeat normally change during sleep?
106712.e: During sleep, the body needs less energy. Nerves then slow down the sinus node, and the heart beats more calmly.
106712.m: The heart beats more slowly during sleep.

106713.q: How does the signal from the sinus node reach the ventricles?
a: As an electrical signal along special fibres
With the blood through the vessels
106713.e: The heart has its own conduction system. Special muscle fibres pass the electrical signal from the sinus node to the ventricles.
106713.m: The heart passes on its rhythm electrically.

106714.q: Which phase mainly gets shorter when the heart beats faster during sport?
106714.e: With a high pulse, it is mainly the filling phase that gets shorter. The pumping phase, by contrast, stays almost the same length.
106714.m: When the heart beats fast, it is mainly diastole that gets shorter.

106715.q: What is a typical sign of a heart attack?
a: Severe pain or pressure in the chest
106715.e: A typical sign is severe pain or pressure behind the breastbone. It can spread to the left arm, the neck or the jaw.
106715.m: Severe chest pain can be a warning sign of a heart attack.

106716.q: How should a person with a suspected heart attack behave until the ambulance arrives?
a: Sit calmly with the upper body raised
106716.e: Rest and a raised upper body take strain off the heart. Any effort increases the oxygen needs of the damaged heart muscle.
106716.m: With a suspected heart attack, the person should sit calmly with the upper body raised.

106717.q: What happens to the blood vessels in working muscles during sport?
106717.e: Working muscles need much more oxygen. That is why their vessels widen, so that more blood can flow through.
106717.m: During sport, wider vessels give the muscles a better blood supply.

106814.q: In Switzerland, how long does the apprenticeship as a forest worker (Forstwart EFZ) take?
106814.e: The basic vocational training takes three years and ends with the Federal VET Diploma (EFZ). Part of the training takes place in inter-company courses.
106814.m: The forest worker apprenticeship takes three years.

106815.q: Which tool does a forest worker use most often to fell trees?
106815.e: With the chainsaw the forest worker fells trees and cuts trunks to length. Using it safely is practised a lot during the apprenticeship.
106815.m: The chainsaw is the forest worker’s most important tool.

106816.q: Why does a forest worker wear chainsaw trousers?
a: They block the saw chain on contact
They protect against rain and snow
They keep your legs warm in winter
106816.e: The trousers contain long fibres that get pulled into the chain on contact and stop the saw in a flash. This prevents serious leg injuries.
106816.m: Chainsaw trousers stop the chainsaw chain in an accident.

106817.q: At what kind of school do people in Switzerland train further to become a forester (Förster HF)?
106817.e: The abbreviation HF stands for Höhere Fachschule, a college of higher education. The usual requirement is a forest worker apprenticeship and a few years of work experience.
106817.m: Foresters train further at a college of higher education.

106818.q: Why do forest workers in the mountains look after the protection forest?
a: It protects villages from avalanches and falling rocks
It makes room for ski runs
106818.e: A healthy mountain forest holds back snow and rocks. Forest workers make sure young trees keep growing there.
106818.m: Protection forest keeps villages safe from avalanches and falling rocks.

106819.q: What is the work called in which forest workers remove weak or troublesome saplings in a young forest?
106819.e: In young forest tending, forest workers help well-grown trees and remove their competitors. This creates a stable, mixed forest.
106819.m: Young forest tending helps the best young trees.

106820.q: Why do forest workers never work completely alone when felling trees?
a: So that someone can help if there is an accident
Because the noise law requires it
Because a chainsaw has two handles
So that the work goes faster
106820.e: Felling trees is one of the most dangerous jobs there is. If there is an accident, someone must be able to give first aid and raise the alarm straight away.
106820.m: For safety reasons you never work alone in the forest.

106821.q: Which headgear is part of a forest worker’s protective equipment?
a: Helmet with ear defenders and visor
Straw hat with a wide brim
106821.e: The forestry helmet protects against falling branches. Ear defenders and visor protect against the noise of the saw and flying chips.
106821.m: Forest workers wear a helmet with ear defenders and a visor.

106822.q: Why do you first saw a wedge-shaped cut into the trunk when felling a tree?
a: So that the tree falls in the direction you want
So that the tree grows faster
So that the resin can run out
So that birds can nest in it
106822.e: The wedge-shaped cut is called the felling notch. It is sawn on the side the tree should fall towards. Then the felling cut is made from the opposite side.
106822.m: The felling notch sets the direction in which the tree falls.

106823.q: Why do you not saw right through the trunk when felling a tree?
a: The strip of wood left standing guides the tree like a hinge
So that the tree can grow back later
Because otherwise the saw goes blunt
So that the tree grows more slowly
106823.e: The narrow strip of wood that is left standing is called the hinge. It works like a hinge and guides the falling trunk in the direction you want.
106823.m: The hinge guides the tree as it falls.

106824.q: In which season is most wood traditionally cut in Switzerland?
106824.e: In winter the sap in the tree is at rest, birds are not nesting, and frozen ground is less damaged by machines.
106824.m: Wood is traditionally cut in winter.

106825.q: In very steep terrain, what is often used to get felled trunks out of the forest?
106825.e: A cable crane pulls the trunks along a supporting cable over steep slopes to a road. In the Alps and foothills this is often the gentlest option.
106825.m: In steep forests a cable crane brings the wood out.

106826.q: What is the machine called that fells trees, strips off the branches and saws them into pieces?
106826.e: The harvester does all the steps with a single gripping head, just as its name suggests. It is used mainly on flat ground.
106826.m: A harvester is a timber harvesting machine.

106827.q: Why may timber harvesting machines only drive on fixed tracks in the forest?
a: So that the rest of the forest floor is not squashed
So that they do not drive too fast
So that hikers can see them better
So that they use less fuel
106827.e: The fixed tracks are called skid trails. If machines only drive there, the rest of the forest floor stays loose, and roots and soil creatures are protected.
106827.m: In the forest, machines only drive on skid trails.

106828.q: Which unit measures the volume of wood in logs without any air gaps?
106828.e: A solid cubic metre equals one cubic metre of solid wood. The timber harvest is measured in this unit.
106828.m: A solid cubic metre is one cubic metre of pure wood.

106829.q: What do you call removing the branches from a felled trunk?
106829.e: When delimbing, the branches are sawn off right at the trunk. Only after that is the trunk cut into pieces.
106829.m: Delimbing means removing the branches from the trunk.

106830.q: What is meant by natural regeneration in a forest?
a: Young trees grow from the seeds of old trees
Trees are cut back every year
106830.e: In natural regeneration, seeds from old trees fall to the ground and sprout there. People do not have to plant anything.
106830.m: In natural regeneration, the forest sows itself.

106831.q: What do young trees on the forest floor need most of all to grow well?
106831.e: That is why foresters thin out the forest on purpose. More sunlight reaches the ground through the gaps in the canopy.
106831.m: Young trees need light to grow.

106832.q: Which tree species, as a shade-tolerant tree, can grow up even under a dense canopy?
106832.e: Young silver firs can tolerate a lot of shade and can wait for decades under old trees until a gap opens.
106832.m: The silver fir grows well even in shade.

106833.q: Which tree species, as a pioneer, is often the first to grow on open land?
106833.e: Birches produce a great many light seeds that the wind carries far. In full sunlight they grow quickly.
106833.m: The birch is a typical pioneer tree species.

106834.q: What is typical of a selection forest (Plenterwald), like those found in the Emmental?
a: Young and old trees grow mixed side by side
All the trees are exactly the same age
The trees stand in straight rows
106834.e: In a selection forest, only single trees are ever harvested. That is why young and old trees stand side by side and the forest keeps renewing itself.
106834.m: In a selection forest, young and old trees stand side by side.

106835.q: Why is natural regeneration usually cheaper than planting?
a: You do not have to buy and plant young trees
The federal government pays for every seedling
You no longer need forestry staff
106835.e: In natural regeneration, the old trees supply the seeds for free. Planting, on the other hand, costs plants, labour and often protective measures.
106835.m: Natural regeneration saves plants and work.

106836.q: Why are naturally regenerated trees usually well adapted to where they grow?
a: Their parents already grew in the same place
They are modified in a laboratory
106836.e: The parent trees have coped with the climate and soil in the same place for decades. Their offspring carry these qualities.
106836.m: Trees from natural regeneration suit their site well.

106837.q: What are old trees called that are deliberately left standing during felling so that they supply the area with seeds?
106837.e: Seed trees scatter their seeds onto the open ground below. Once enough young trees have grown, they are often harvested later too.
106837.m: Seed trees supply an area with new seeds.

106838.q: What is a mast year in a forest?
a: A year with a particularly large number of seeds
A year with a particularly large amount of felling
A year with no rain at all
A year in which wild animals are fed
106838.e: In mast years, trees such as beech or oak bear an unusually large amount of fruit. Afterwards, a particularly large number of young trees sprout.
106838.m: In a mast year, trees produce a great many seeds.

106839.e: In afforestation, people plant young trees, for example after storm damage or on former pastures. Unlike natural regeneration, they choose the tree species.
106839.m: Afforestation means planting a new forest.

106840.q: Where are young trees raised for afforestation?
106840.e: In forest tree nurseries, the young plants grow from seed until they are strong enough to be planted out in the forest.
106840.m: Young plants for the forest are raised in a tree nursery.

106841.q: After which natural events did Switzerland begin large-scale reforestation of cleared mountain slopes in the 19th century?
106841.e: Bare mountain slopes could no longer hold back rainwater. After major floods, for example in 1868, people recognised the protective effect of forests.
106841.m: Forest on steep slopes protects against floods.

106842.q: What are the young trees called that are put into the ground during afforestation?
106842.e: Saplings are usually two to four years old when they are planted. They are put into the ground with a planting spade or a hoe.

106843.q: Why are barriers often built as well when reforesting steep avalanche slopes?
a: So that snow does not sweep the young trees away
So that tourists can climb there
So that wild animals find shelter
So that the ground gets warmer
106843.e: Young trees cannot yet stop moving snow. Barriers protect them until the forest itself works as a protection forest.

106844.q: What does the law usually require when forest may be removed for a building project?
106844.e: For every approved clearance, the same amount of forest must in principle be planted again, usually in the same area. This way the forest area is preserved.
106844.m: Cleared forest must usually be replaced.

106845.q: Why were almost only spruces often planted in afforestation on the Swiss Plateau in the past?
a: They grow fast and provide building timber
They are especially firm against storms
106845.e: Spruces promised a quick yield. Today we know that pure spruce stands in the lowlands are often not very stable.
106845.m: Pure spruce forests grow fast but are vulnerable.

106846.q: Which trees are preferably planted in afforestation today?
a: A mixture of species suited to the site
106846.e: Mixed forests of tree species that suit the site spread the risk. If one species fails, the others remain standing.

106847.q: According to the Forest Act, what usually has to be done if forest may be cleared as an exception?
a: Leave the land unused for ever
Build a wall around the area
Nothing more, the permit is enough
106847.e: For an approved clearance, a replacement must usually be provided in the same area, mostly as new forest. This way Switzerland's forest area is preserved.
106847.m: Anyone who clears forest usually has to plant new forest.

106848.q: Who is mainly responsible for enforcing the Forest Act in Switzerland?
106848.e: The federal government sets out the principles, and the cantons put them into practice with their own forestry services. For example, they approve fellings.
106848.m: The cantons put the Forest Act into practice.

106849.q: What does the Forest Act basically forbid?
106849.e: Forest clearance is turning forest permanently into other land, such as building land. An exception needs a permit for important reasons.
106849.m: In Switzerland, forest may basically not be cleared.

106850.q: According to the Forest Act, what may everyone do in a Swiss forest?
106850.e: The forest is meant to be open to the public. This also applies to privately owned forest.
106850.m: Anyone may enter the Swiss forest.

106851.q: What is basically not allowed in the forest and on forest roads?
106851.e: Motor vehicles may only use forests and forest roads for forestry work. There are special rules for exceptions.
106851.m: You may not drive into the forest by car.

106852.q: According to the Forest Act, what basically applies to forest that has grown by itself on an abandoned pasture?
a: It may be removed at any time
It automatically belongs to the federal government
106852.e: What matters is whether an area is actually covered with trees and fulfils forest functions. That is why newly grown forest is also basically protected.
106852.m: Forest that grew by itself is also forest in the eyes of the law.

106853.q: What does the Forest Act say about Switzerland's forest area?
a: It is to be doubled by 2050
It is set anew every year
106853.e: The forest is to be preserved in its area and its geographical distribution. This principle of forest conservation is at the heart of the law.
106853.m: The Swiss forest is not to get smaller.

106854.q: Which federal office is responsible for forests in Switzerland?
106854.e: The FOEN is the federal government's specialist office for forests. It prepares the groundwork and supports projects in the forest.
106854.m: The FOEN looks after the forest at federal level.

106855.q: Why was so much wood needed in the time of Hans Carl von Carlowitz?
a: For heating, building, and for mines and smelting furnaces
106855.e: Around 1700, wood was the most important fuel and building material. Mines and smelting works used huge amounts, so many forests were cleared completely.
106855.m: Around 1700, wood was the most important fuel and building material.

106856.q: What was the famous book by Hans Carl von Carlowitz about?
a: The forest and the use of wood
106856.e: In his “Sylvicultura oeconomica” of 1713, Carlowitz wrote about how to use the forest without destroying it.
106856.m: Carlowitz wrote a book about the forest.

106857.q: Which problem did Carlowitz warn about in his book?
106857.e: Mines, smelting works and towns used huge amounts of wood. Carlowitz feared that soon there would not be enough of it.
106857.m: Carlowitz warned of a shortage of wood.

106858.q: What fits Carlowitz's idea of sustainable forest use?
a: Planting young trees to replace felled ones
Felling the whole forest at once
Leaving felled areas empty for ever
106858.e: Carlowitz wanted the forest to last. So bare areas were to be replanted, and no more wood was to be cut than grows back.
106858.m: Sustainable means the forest is preserved even though it is used.

106859.q: Which word used by Carlowitz later developed into the German term for “sustainability” (Nachhaltigkeit)?
106859.e: Carlowitz called for a “continuirliche beständige und nachhaltende Nutzung” (continuous, lasting and sustaining use) of the forest. The word Nachhaltigkeit, sustainability, later came from this.
106859.m: Carlowitz spoke of a “nachhaltende”, sustaining use of the forest.

106860.q: Apart from using wood sparingly, what did Carlowitz recommend against the wood shortage?
106860.e: Carlowitz called for cleared areas to be stocked with trees again. In addition, better stoves were to use less wood.
106860.m: Carlowitz wanted to renew the forest by sowing and planting.

106861.q: When did Hans Carl von Carlowitz live?
106861.e: Carlowitz was born in 1645 and died in 1714. So he lived in the Baroque period.

106862.q: Which principle of forest use is mainly associated with Carlowitz today?
a: Cut only as much wood as grows back
Cut as much wood as possible at once
Fell only broadleaved trees, never conifers
106862.e: Carlowitz called for a balance between using wood and regrowth. This idea is at the heart of the principle of sustainability.
106862.m: Sustainable means not using more than grows back.

106863.q: What is the bark beetle called that causes the greatest forest damage in Switzerland?
106863.e: The European spruce bark beetle is only about half a centimetre long. But it can multiply in huge numbers.
106863.m: The European spruce bark beetle is Switzerland's most dangerous bark beetle.

106864.q: Which tree species does the European spruce bark beetle mainly attack?
106864.e: This beetle specialises in this conifer. Weakened trees at low altitudes are especially at risk.
106864.m: The European spruce bark beetle mainly attacks spruces.

106865.q: Where does the bark beetle make its breeding tunnels?
a: Between the bark and the wood
106865.e: The female lays her eggs in tunnels just under the bark. From there, the larvae eat side tunnels that form a typical pattern.
106865.m: Bark beetles breed just under the bark.

106866.q: Why does a tree badly infested by bark beetles die?
a: The tunnels cut off its flow of sap
The beetle eats all the needles
The tree becomes too heavy and topples over
106866.e: The feeding tunnels destroy the thin layer that carries water and nutrients. The crown is no longer supplied and dries out.
106866.m: Bark beetles cut off the tree's supply.

106867.q: How does a healthy spruce defend itself against bark beetles boring in?
106867.e: When a beetle bores in, sticky resin flows out. It can glue the beetle up or push it back out.

106868.q: Which weather helps bark beetles multiply in huge numbers?
106868.e: Warmth lets the beetles produce several generations a year more quickly. At the same time, the trees are weakened by lack of water.
106868.m: Heat and drought help bark beetles.

106869.q: What is the most important measure when a bark beetle infestation is discovered?
a: Quickly fell the infested trees and remove them
Water the tree heavily every day
106869.e: If infested spruces are quickly taken out of the forest or debarked, the young beetles cannot fly out. This slows down the spread.
106869.m: Infested trees must leave the forest quickly.

106870.q: From the outside, how can you often first spot a fresh bark beetle infestation?
a: By brown boring dust on the trunk
By red flowers in the crown
By white mould on the needles
By an unusually large number of cones
106870.e: Boring dust looks like fine ground coffee and collects in cracks in the bark and at the foot of the trunk. Later the crown changes colour.
106870.m: Brown boring dust gives bark beetles away.

106871.q: What are bark beetles lured into special traps with?
106871.e: Pheromones are scents the beetles use to attract one another. The traps are mainly used to monitor the number of beetles.
106871.m: Bark beetle traps work with lures.

106872.q: How much wood did Lothar blow down in Switzerland in 1999, compared with a normal annual harvest?
a: Almost three times an annual harvest
About a tenth of an annual harvest
About a hundredth of an annual harvest
106872.e: Lothar blew down about 13 million cubic metres of wood. That was almost three times as much as was harvested in Switzerland in a year at the time.
106872.m: Lothar blew down almost three annual harvests of wood.

106873.q: Which insects multiplied in huge numbers in the storm-felled wood in the years after Lothar?
106873.e: Fallen and weakened spruces offered ideal breeding places. As a result, many more trees died in the following years.
106873.m: After Lothar, bark beetles spread widely.

106874.q: In 1999, the storm Lothar blew down whole forests. What is such storm damage in a forest called?
106874.e: In windthrow, a storm blows trees over, roots and all, or snaps them. Lothar caused huge areas of windthrow in Switzerland.
106874.m: Trees blown over by a storm are called windthrow.

106875.q: Which areas of Switzerland did Lothar hit hardest?
a: The Swiss Plateau and the Prealps
The Engadine and the Val Poschiavo
106875.e: Lothar moved in from the west across the north side of the Alps. Especially in the cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Lucerne, whole forests lay on the ground.
106875.m: Lothar mainly hit the Swiss Plateau and the Prealps.

106876.q: Why was Lothar still dangerous even after the storm?
a: Clearing up led to fatal accidents
The roads stayed closed for years
106876.e: Fallen trees are often under great tension. When they are sawn up, trunks can spring up unexpectedly, which is why several people died during the clearing work.
106876.m: Clearing up storm-felled wood is very dangerous.

106877.q: Why did a particularly large number of spruces fall during the storm Lothar?
a: They lose their needles in winter
106877.e: Spruces form a flat root plate, especially on wet soils. So in strong wind they easily topple over, roots and all.
106877.m: Spruces have shallow roots and are easily blown over.

106878.q: What happened on many areas flattened by Lothar in the years that followed?
a: Young forest grew back without planting
They have stayed bare to this day
106878.e: Researchers observed that on many areas young trees quickly came up by themselves. The new forest was often more mixed than the old one.
106878.m: New forest often grows by itself on storm-damaged areas.

106879.q: What happened to the price of wood after the storm Lothar?
a: Wood could no longer be sold
106879.e: Suddenly there was far more wood in the forest than the sawmills could process. The large supply made prices collapse.
106879.m: After Lothar, the price of wood fell sharply.

106880.q: How was much of the storm-felled wood protected from fungi and insects after Lothar?
a: It was constantly sprinkled with water
It was buried in the ground
106880.e: In so-called wet storage sites, sprinklers keep the wood constantly damp. That way fungi and beetles cannot attack it.
106880.m: Wet storage keeps wood damp and so protects it.

106881.q: What is chopped-up wood called that is burnt automatically in large heating systems?
106881.e: For wood chips, branches, treetops and leftover wood are chopped into small pieces. Many municipalities heat school buildings with them.
106881.m: Wood chips are chopped-up wood for heating.

106882.q: Why is heating with wood from sustainable forestry considered almost carbon-neutral?
a: The tree absorbed the CO2 while growing
Wood burns with no exhaust gases at all
106882.e: When it burns, about as much CO2 is released as the tree took in from the air before. If the same amount of forest grows back, the balance stays almost even.
106882.m: When burnt, wood releases the CO2 it absorbed while growing.

106883.q: Why should firewood be well dried before burning?
a: It gives more heat and less smoke
Wet wood burns far too hot
106883.e: In wet wood, the water must evaporate first, and that takes energy. Wet wood also smokes and produces more soot.

106884.q: What is the unit for one cubic metre of stacked firewood with gaps?
106884.e: A stere is a cube with sides of one metre, filled with stacked logs. Because there is air in between, it contains less wood than a solid cubic metre.
106884.m: A stere is one cubic metre of stacked wood.

106885.q: Which pollutant is mainly produced by badly operated wood-burning systems?
106885.e: Incomplete burning produces tiny particles of soot and dust. They can get deep into the lungs.
106885.m: Badly burning wood fires produce a lot of fine dust.

106886.q: What is a network of pipes called that delivers hot water from a central wood-fired heating plant to many houses?
106886.e: The heat is produced in a large heating plant and distributed through insulated pipes. That way the individual houses do not need their own stove.
106886.m: A district heating network distributes heat to many houses.

106887.q: Which stove stores the heat of a wood fire in heavy stones and gives it off for hours?
106887.e: The fire heats up the thick walls of stone and ceramic. They give off heat long after the fire has gone out.
106887.m: A tiled stove stores heat for a long time.

106888.q: What causes most forest fires in Switzerland?
106888.e: Discarded cigarettes, unattended fires or sparks from machines cause most fires.
106888.m: Most forest fires are caused by people.

106889.q: Which Swiss canton has the most forest fires?
106889.e: On the south side of the Alps the climate is mild, and there are long dry spells again and again. Many slopes are also steep and hard to reach.
106889.m: Forest fires are most frequent in Ticino.

106890.q: In which season are forest fires particularly common in Ticino?
106890.e: At that time dry leaves lie on the ground, the plants are not yet green, and a dry north wind often blows.
106890.m: In Ticino, late winter is forest fire season.

106891.q: What usually grows back first on an area burnt by a forest fire?
a: Nothing at all for a hundred years
106891.e: On the burnt area above Leuk in the Valais, which burnt in 2003, herbs, grasses and shrubs grew first. It takes decades before a forest stands there again.
106891.m: After a forest fire, herbs and shrubs come back first.

106892.q: How do helicopters fight forest fires on steep ground?
a: With a water container on a rope
106892.e: The helicopters fill the container in a lake or river and release the water right over the fire.
106892.m: Firefighting helicopters fetch water from lakes and rivers.

106893.q: What do the authorities often order when the risk of forest fires is high?
a: A ban on fires in the forest
A ban on swimming in lakes
106893.e: In dry weather, a single spark can start a fire. Then fire is banned in and near the forest, often even in permanent fireplaces.
106893.m: In dry weather, there is often a ban on fires in the forest.

106894.q: Which natural event can start a forest fire without any human involvement?
106894.e: If lightning strikes a tree, dry wood can catch fire. Such fires start mainly during summer thunderstorms.

106895.q: Why are forest fires on steep mountain slopes particularly problematic?
a: Afterwards protection from natural hazards is missing
Afterwards the ground freezes for ever
Afterwards no animal can live there any more
106895.e: Burnt slopes can no longer slow down rockfall, avalanches and debris flows. It takes decades for a new protection forest to grow back.
106895.m: After a fire, the protection forest is often missing.

106896.q: What is meant by browsing damage?
a: Wild animals eat the buds and shoots of young trees
Wild animals rub their antlers on trunks
Woodpeckers peck holes in the bark
106896.e: In browsing, animals such as roe deer or red deer nibble off the tips of young trees. Especially in winter, they find little other food.
106896.m: Browsing is wild animals eating young shoots.

106897.q: Which wild animal causes the most browsing damage on the Swiss Plateau?
106897.e: Roe deer are very common on the Swiss Plateau. They like to feed on buds and young shoots.
106897.m: On the Swiss Plateau, browsing is mainly caused by roe deer.

106898.q: Which conifer species suffers particularly badly from browsing in Switzerland?
106898.e: Wild animals prefer to eat young silver firs. In some forests, hardly any young firs grow up any more.
106898.m: Wild animals particularly like to browse silver firs.

106899.q: Why is it particularly harmful when wild animals eat the leading shoot of a young tree?
a: The young tree hardly grows any taller
The young tree stops forming flowers
The young tree loses its roots
The young tree turns brown at once
106899.e: The leading shoot is the top shoot that makes the tree grow upwards. If it is eaten again and again, the young tree stays small and bushy.
106899.m: Without a leading shoot, a young tree hardly grows upwards.

106900.q: How can individual young trees be protected from browsing?
a: With wire cages or tree shelters
With salt licks put up nearby
106900.e: The shelters stop roe deer and red deer from reaching the shoots. Once the tree is big enough, they are removed again.
106900.m: Wire cages protect young trees from browsing.

106901.q: What effect does heavy browsing have on the make-up of a forest?
a: Fewer different tree species grow up
The forest becomes richer in species
106901.e: Wild animals prefer to eat certain tree species. The less popular species are left, and the forest becomes more uniform.
106901.m: Heavy browsing makes the forest poorer in species.

106902.q: Which measure do the cantons use to regulate wild animal numbers and limit browsing?
106902.e: Hunting plans take into account the state of the young forest. The aim is a balance between forest and wildlife.
106902.m: Hunting helps keep forest and wildlife in balance.

106903.q: Which large wild animal with antlers causes a lot of browsing, especially in mountain forests?
106903.e: Red deer often live in herds and in winter eat buds, shoots and even bark. In the Grisons, their numbers are large.
106903.m: Red deer cause a lot of browsing in mountain forests.

106904.q: What is the Swiss National Forest Inventory?
a: A regular survey of the state of the forest
A list of all foresters in Switzerland
A forest festival in every canton
106904.e: For the National Forest Inventory, trees are measured and counted all over the country. That way we know how the Swiss forest is doing.
106904.m: The National Forest Inventory shows the state of the Swiss forest.

106905.q: Why is the National Forest Inventory repeated every few years?
a: To detect changes in the forest
Because the trees move every year
Because the old figures get lost
106905.e: The first inventory was made in the 1980s. Repeating it shows whether the forest is growing, how much wood grows back and how biodiversity is doing.
106905.m: Repeated measurements show how the forest is changing.

106906.q: How does the growing stock per hectare in the Swiss forest compare with the rest of Europe?
106906.e: Many Swiss forests are dense and old because less wood is used than grows back. That is why there is a particularly large amount of wood per hectare.
106906.m: There is a great deal of wood per hectare in the Swiss forest.

106907.q: Which feature relating to biodiversity does the National Forest Inventory also record?
106907.e: Dead trees are a habitat for beetles, fungi, mosses and woodpeckers. That is why their amount is an important sign of how natural a forest is.

106908.q: What does the growing stock of a forest indicate?
a: The volume of all living trunks
The amount of firewood in storage
The weight of all the leaves
106908.e: The growing stock is given in cubic metres. It shows how much wood is standing in the forest right now.
106908.m: The growing stock is the wood standing in the forest.

106909.q: How does the National Forest Inventory obtain its data?
106909.e: Sample plots on a regular grid are visited all over the country and the trees are measured. Aerial photos and surveys of the forestry services are added to this.
106909.m: The National Forest Inventory measures trees on many sample plots.

106910.q: How has Switzerland's forest area developed in recent decades?
a: It has increased, especially in the Alps
It has stayed exactly the same
It has increased only in towns
106910.e: Shrubs and trees grow by themselves on abandoned alpine pastures and mountain meadows. That way new forest gradually forms there.
106910.m: The Swiss forest is growing, especially in the Alps.

106911.q: Who owns most of the Swiss forest?
106911.e: About two thirds of the forest belongs to municipalities, civic communities, corporations or cantons. The rest is mostly privately owned in small plots.
106911.m: Most of the Swiss forest belongs to public bodies.

106912.q: At what height is the diameter of a tree trunk measured in forest inventories?
a: In the middle of the trunk
106912.e: This is called the diameter at breast height. Because it is always measured at the same height, the values can be compared well.
106912.m: The trunk diameter is measured at breast height.

107013.q: Which blood vessels are the finest in the human body?
107013.e: Capillaries, also called hair vessels, are the smallest blood vessels. They form a fine network that runs through almost all tissues.
107013.m: The capillaries are the finest blood vessels in the body.

107014.q: How thick is the wall of a capillary?
107014.e: The wall of a capillary is made of just one thin layer of endothelial cells. That is why substances can pass through it easily.
107014.m: Capillaries have a wafer-thin wall of just one layer of cells.

107015.q: What is the main job of the capillaries?
a: Exchanging substances between blood and tissue
107015.e: In the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood into the tissue. In return, the blood takes up carbon dioxide and waste.
107015.m: In the capillaries, blood and tissue exchange substances.

107016.q: Roughly what is the diameter of a typical capillary?
107016.e: Capillaries are only about 5 to 10 micrometres wide, which is much thinner than a hair. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre.
107016.m: A capillary is much thinner than a human hair.

107017.q: How do red blood cells move through the narrowest capillaries?
a: Not at all, they stay still
107017.e: The narrowest capillaries are hardly wider than a red blood cell. The blood cells change shape and squeeze through one at a time.
107017.m: In narrow capillaries, red blood cells line up one by one.

107018.q: Between which blood vessels do the capillaries lie?
a: Between the windpipe and the lungs
Between the stomach and the intestines
107018.e: The blood flows from the arteries through the fine capillaries into the veins and from there back to the heart.
107018.m: The capillaries connect arteries and veins.

107019.q: Which gas do the capillaries in a working muscle mainly give off?
107019.e: The blood brings oxygen to the muscle cells, which need it to make energy. In return the blood takes up carbon dioxide.
107019.m: In muscles, the capillaries give oxygen to the cells.

107020.q: Where do capillaries in the lungs take up oxygen?
107020.e: The air sacs (alveoli) are surrounded by dense networks of capillaries. There, oxygen passes from the air you breathe into the blood.
107020.m: A network of capillaries surrounds the air sacs in the lungs.

107021.q: How fast does blood flow in the capillaries compared with the large arteries?
107021.e: All the capillaries together have a huge total cross-section, so the blood flows very slowly there. This leaves enough time for substances to be exchanged.
107021.m: Blood flows slowly in the capillaries so that the exchange can happen.

107022.q: What is the large artery in the groin that supplies the leg with blood called?
107022.e: The femoral artery, in Latin arteria femoralis, runs from the groin down the thigh. It is the main artery of the leg.
107022.m: The leg is mainly supplied by the femoral artery.

107023.q: Which artery is squeezed by the cuff when blood pressure is measured?
a: The brachial artery in the upper arm
107023.e: The cuff goes round the upper arm and squeezes the artery there. Its Latin name is arteria brachialis.
107023.m: When measuring blood pressure, the upper arm artery is briefly squeezed.

107024.q: Which artery runs along the little-finger side of the forearm?
107024.e: The forearm has two main arteries along its two bones. The ulna is on the little-finger side, and the ulnar artery runs next to it.
107024.m: The ulnar artery runs next to the ulna on the little-finger side.

107025.q: On which side of the wrist do you usually feel for the pulse?
a: On the back of the hand
In the middle of the palm
107025.e: On the thumb side of the wrist, the radial artery runs just under the skin. There the pulse can easily be felt with two fingers.
107025.m: You feel the pulse at the wrist on the thumb side.

107026.q: How does blood pressure change the further the blood gets from the heart?
a: It stays exactly the same everywhere
107026.e: The heart creates the pressure, and some of it is constantly lost through friction in the ever finer vessels. In the veins, the pressure is finally very low.
107026.m: The further from the heart, the lower the blood pressure.

107027.e: The pulmonary artery takes oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is still an artery, because it carries blood away from the heart.
107027.m: The pulmonary artery is an artery with oxygen-poor blood.

107028.q: Why do arteries have thicker walls than veins?
a: The blood pressure in them is higher
They lie right under the skin
107028.e: The heart pumps the blood into the arteries at high pressure. Their thick, muscular walls withstand this pressure.
107028.m: Arteries have thick walls because of the high pressure.

107029.q: What are the smallest branches of the arteries called?
107029.e: Arterioles are tiny arteries that lead the blood into the hair vessels. By getting narrower or wider, they control the blood supply.
107029.m: The smallest arteries are called arterioles.

107030.q: Which painless examination is used to check the carotid artery for narrowing?
107030.e: With an ultrasound device, the carotid artery can be viewed from outside and the blood flow measured. This shows narrowing without any operation.
107030.m: Narrowing of the carotid artery is found with ultrasound.

107031.q: How many common carotid arteries does a person have?
107031.e: There is a left and a right common carotid artery. Each supplies its own side of the head and neck.
107031.m: People have one carotid artery on the left and one on the right.

107032.q: Where can you feel the pulse well on the neck?
a: At the side of the neck, on the carotid artery
At the back of the neck, on the spine
At the front, on the voice box
Under the chin, on the bone
107032.e: The carotid artery lies at the side of the neck just under the skin. If you put two fingers there, you feel the blood throbbing with every heartbeat.
107032.m: At the side of the neck you can feel the pulse of the carotid artery.

107033.q: Into which two branches does the common carotid artery split?
